items.title: Government to invest $1bn in Pwalugu multipurpose dam, first phase expected by 2029
items.description: Government is planning to invest US$1 billion in the full completion of the Pwalugu Multipurpose Dam, as part of efforts to boost agricultural production, expand agro-processing and strengthen energy supply. Presenting the 2027 Budget Statement in Parliament, Finance Minister, Dr Ato Forson said the project will support large-scale vegetable production, aquaculture, irrigation and hydropower generation. He said the dam will provide water for about 25,000 hectares of land dedicated to vegetable production, while its reservoir will accommodate 100,000 fish cages to support aquaculture. According to Dr Forson, the project is expected to promote year-round agricultural production, improve water security and provide flood protection across the White Volta corridor. The dam will also generate 77 megawatts of hydropower to support agro-industrial activities within and around the Pwalugu enclave. “Pwalugu will support year-round vegetable production, flood protection, water security, agriculture and agribusiness across the dry water corridor,” he told Parliament. He explained that the electricity generated will support processing factories, irrigation systems, pack houses and cold storage facilities, helping farmers and businesses add value to agricultural produce closer to production centres. The Finance Minister said the project will be implemented in phases, with the first phase expected to be ready by early 2029 and full completion scheduled for December 2030. “The first phase of the Pwalugu Multipurpose Dam will be ready by early 2029, with full completion by December 2030,” Dr Forson stated. He added that the dam will be complemented by service vegetable enclaves in other regions, water harvesting systems and protected cultivation to expand agricultural production. The investment forms part of government’s broader New Economy Programme, which seeks to transform commercial agriculture, strengthen local industries and create employment opportunities.

items.title: ‎Nigeria has left ’emergency ward,’ targets $1trn economy by 2030 – Tinubu
items.description: ‎ ‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ‎ President Bola Tinubu on Thursday declared that Nigeria’s economy has moved “from stabilisation to shared prosperity,” citing non-oil exports above $6 billion, external reserves of about $55 billion, and a target of a $1 trillion economy by 2030. ‎ ‎Speaking at the public presentation of Economic Diversification and Structural Transformation in Nigeria: Past, Present and Future, authored by Honourable Abdulmumin Jibrin Kofa, Tinubu said the country had abandoned “cosmetic remedies” for what he called the “hard road of surgery.” ‎ ‎According to him: “For too long, Nigeria’s story was a song sung in a single note. We were a nation of boundless promise tied to a single product, our budget, our currency and the livelihoods of millions rising and falling with the tides of a distant oil market. We floated on the fragile illusion of oil wealth while the foundations beneath us crackborders. ‎ ‎”When I took the oath of office, I did not inherit a calm sea; I inherited a gathering storm: a collapsing naira, debt service that swallowed nearly all our revenue, depleted reserves, a fuel subsidy that bled our treasury dry, and factories falling silent as industries and jobs fled across our borders.” ‎ ‎The President said his administration inherited “a gathering storm,” including “a collapsing naira, debt service that swallowed nearly all our revenue, depleted reserves, a fuel subsidy that bled our treasury dry, and factories falling silent.” ‎ ‎“We chose reform over ruin. We removed the fuel subsidy. We unified the exchange rate. These were not easy decisions, and I know the weight they placed on every household. But they were necessary, and today the pain is yielding its promise.” ‎ ‎He stated that non-oil activities now account for about 96 per cent of Gross Domestic Product, while non-oil exports have crossed $6 billion, which he described as the highest in Nigeria’s history. ‎ ‎Tinubu also said external reserves had risen to about $55 billion, representing “more than fourteen months of import cover,” and that non-oil revenue had grown from ₦13.63 trillion in 2023 to ₦16.4 trillion in the first half of 2026. ‎ ‎The President said government alone cannot build a $1 trillion economy, adding that wealth must be created by enterprises that “invest, innovate, manufacture and export.” ‎ ‎“Our duty is to clear the path before them,” he said. “That is why our 2025 budget introduced a first-of-its-kind De-risking Framework to draw in private capital, which we expect to provide 86 per cent of the investment our 2030 goal demands.” ‎ ‎He said the administration was harmonising taxes and ending “the menace of multiple taxation.” ‎“We cannot tax our way into prosperity; we must produce our way there,” Tinubu said. ‎ ‎The President said the administration had “fought for Mambilla,” winning a $3.38 billion arbitration at the International Chamber of Commerce in Paris and freeing “a project held hostage for more than nine years.” ‎He added that Geregu Power is moving to raise its capacity to 1,300 megawatts, while the Port Harcourt and Warri refineries are “stirring back to life.” ‎ ‎On infrastructure, Tinubu listed the Kano–Katsina–Maradi railway, Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway, Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway, Abuja–Kaduna–Kano Expressway, East–West Road, Ibadan–Ife–Ilesa Expressway, Port Harcourt–Enugu and Enugu–Onitsha expressways, and the restoration of Carter Bridge. ‎ ‎He said 52 per cent of legacy highway mileage is in the North and 48 per cent in the South. ‎ ‎“We are building fairly and deliberately, so that no zone is left behind and no citizen is a stranger to opportunity,” he said. ‎ ‎Tinubu said more than 10,000 homes are rising across 14 states and the Federal Capital Territory under the Renewed Hope Cities and Estates Programme. ‎He said the MOFI Real Estate Investment Fund had provided about ₦128 billion in mortgages to 1,859 families in 25 states, at a fixed rate of 9.75 per cent over 20 years. ‎ ‎“As this market grows, so must the confidence of those who invest in it,” he said. “I will therefore work hand in hand with the National Assembly and stakeholders to establish a strong regulatory authority for housing and real estate.” ‎ ‎The President also cited NELFUND, university solarisation, Bank of Industry loans and grants across all 774 local government areas, the 3MTT digital-skills programme, and 90,000 kilometres of fibre-optic infrastructure. ‎“Roads and power lines are the skeleton of a nation; its people are its life,” he said. ‎ ‎Tinubu commended Jibrin, the member representing Kiru/Bebeji Federal Constituency in Kano State, whose years as a lawmaker and chairman of key National Assembly committees, including Finance and Appropriations, “lend these pages the weight of experience.” ‎ ‎“This is the essence of the book we present today,” Tinubu said. “It looks back with honesty, looks around with clarity and looks ahead with courage.” ‎ ‎He said: “The days of hardship are temporary; the foundations we are laying are permanent. Let us keep building until the world looks upon Nigeria and sees not promise deferred, but promise fulfilled.” ‎ ‎The event was held at the State House Conference Centre in Abuja, with Governor Charles Soludo as keynote speaker, Alhaji Abdulsamad Isyaku Rabiu as book presenter and Dr Reuben Abati as reviewer. items.title: Trafic de drogue à Tunis | Un réseau international démantelé et trois dealers arrêtés
items.description: Un réseau international de trafic de stupéfiants opérant notamment à Tunis a été démantelé et trois de ses membres ont été arrêtés et placés en détention. L'enquête a été menée par les unités de la brigade des recherches et d'investigation de Tunis, en coordination avec la direction des renseignements et des recherches de la Garde nationale, et a abouti à l'interpellation de trois principaux membres de ce réseau criminel. Parmi les suspects, on compte deux ressortissants tunisiens récidivistes et faisant déjà l'objet d'avis de recherche, ainsi qu'un individu de nationalité étrangère spécialisé dans l'acheminement illicite de cannabis en Tunisie, précise une source sécuritaire citée par l'agence TAP, ce jeudi 12 novembre 2026. L'intervention a également permis de saisir une importante quantité de stupéfiants ainsi qu'une somme d'argent provenant des revenus de cette activité illicite. Le ministère public a ordonné la mise en détention des trois suspects alors que l'enquête se poursuit, ajoute la même source. Y. N. Ph. items.title: Government targets self-sufficiency in sugar production by 2030
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson says Ghana will pursue self-sufficiency in sugar production by 2030 as part of efforts to reduce dependence on imports and strengthen domestic agro-industrial production. Presenting the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy to Parliament on Thursday, November 12, 2026, he identified the sugar industry as one of eight integrated agro-industrial sectors under the government’s New Economy programme. “Ghana will pursue self-sufficiency in sugar requirements by 2030,” he said. The target forms part of the government’s broader plan to expand local production, promote value addition and create jobs through agro-industrial development. Ghana currently relies heavily on imported sugar to meet domestic demand, despite the potential for local production. The government is expected to outline specific measures for achieving the 2030 target as it develops its plans for the sugar industry.

items.title: 2027: Tinubu will lose if he contests against anybody picked on street — Dalung
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye African Democratic Congress (ADC) chieftain Solomon Dalung has expressed confidence that President Bola Tinubu would lose the 2027 election even if his opponent were “anybody picked on the street,” arguing that the President was afraid of facing voters. Speaking on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Thursday, Dalung made the prediction while responding to a question about how the opposition could overcome the APC’s resources amid the current internal leadership and legal crisis in the ADC. He nevertheless insisted the party was ready to challenge Tinubu at the ballot. “Since my experience in politics, like I always say, Nigerians, I was brought into politics at a much tender age. I have never seen a weak president in an election like Bola Ahmed Tinubu. If you drag anybody on the street and put him on a ballot at a contest with Tinubu, he will defeat him,” Dalung said. He claimed Tinubu was apprehensive about the election despite having been in office for four years, and challenged the President and APC to let the contest be decided by voters. “Bola Tinubu is so scared, having been in office for four years, he is so scared of election. And all we are seeing in ADC, let’s meet at the ballot. You claim it was the ballot that brought you to power, let’s meet at the ballot,” he said. Dalung also accused the APC of obstructing opposition parties’ campaign activities, alleging that venues had been closed, hotels taken over and party offices sealed. He compared the situation with the 2014 election period, saying the APC would have been left with few places to campaign if it had faced similar restrictions then. “Nobody will be blamed except Tinubu. Why? Because I mean, in the history of Nigeria, we have seen opposition parties contest election, but we have never seen this type of situation. If the PDP in 2014 were closing venues for rallies and taking over hotels, sealing party offices, the APC would have no place to campaign except the streets,” he said. He argued that moving the opposition onto the streets would not weaken its campaign, claiming those attending its gatherings were genuine supporters rather than people hired to fill rallies. “Now, for Tinubu and his APC to move the opposition on pit, they have lost the election. This is because the people we are having on the street are organic followers. Those are the Nigerians that will vote. They are not rented crowds from all over the federation,” Dalung said. items.title: Gov’t targets aquaculture expansion to address 500,000-tonne fish supply gap – Finance Minister
items.description: The government plans to expand aquaculture production and restore marine and inland fisheries as part of efforts to address Ghana’s annual fish supply gap of about 500,000 metric tonnes. The Minister for Finance, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, announced the measures while presenting the 2027 Budget in Parliament on Thursday, November 12. He said aquaculture would become the principal source of new fish supply, with commercial and smallholder operators receiving support to increase production. “Mr Speaker, Ghana has an annual estimated fish supply gap of about 500,000 metric tonnes. Mr Speaker, this is not acceptable. We will fix this,” he said. Under the plan, the Minister said that aquaculture clusters will receive quality broodstock, fingerlings, feed, cages, ponds, tanks, aquatic health laboratories and systems for disease surveillance and water quality management. Dr Forson said the government would also provide access to patient financing and insurance to help responsible aquaculture operators expand their businesses. He added that fish production would be linked to cold-chain facilities, hygienic processing, testing, transportation and assured markets to reduce post-harvest losses and improve the distribution of fish. The government also plans to establish modern fish villages and landing sites across the country. On fisheries management, the Finance Minister said measures would be introduced to tackle illegal fishing, strengthen the licensing regime and involve local communities in protecting the country’s fisheries resources. “We will increase fish supply without destroying the resources on which future supply depends,” he said.

items.title: Reps condemn political violence as thugs attack NDC supporters in Lagos; NDC, APC-PCC fault attack
items.description: By By Henry Umoru, and Gift ChapiOdekina The House of Representatives, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and the All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council (APC-PCC) have condemned reported cases of political violence across the country following an attack on NDC supporters during a town hall meeting in Lagos. While the NDC demanded an immediate investigation, arrest and prosecution of those responsible for the attack in Lagos, the APC-PCC also condemned the incident and called on security agencies to apprehend the perpetrators. The Lagos State chapter of the APC equally condemned the reported attack but denied any involvement, challenging the NDC to provide credible evidence linking the ruling party to the incident. The House of Representatives, on Wednesday, also resolved to investigate reported attacks, intimidation and disruption of political activities across the country ahead of the 2027 general elections. The resolution followed the adoption of a motion of urgent public importance sponsored by the House Minority Leader, Rep. Fred Agbedi, and 16 other lawmakers, amid growing concerns over attacks on political meetings, rallies and processions in different parts of the country. Presenting the motion on behalf of the sponsors, Agbedi condemned acts of violence, intimidation, assault and destruction of property associated with political activities, irrespective of the political parties or individuals affected. He appealed to political parties, candidates and their supporters to reject inflammatory rhetoric, discourage violence and cooperate with security agencies to maintain public peace. Citing Section 40 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, the Minority Leader reminded lawmakers that Nigerians were guaranteed the right to assemble freely and associate with others, including the right to form or belong to political parties. He also cited the constitutional provision which makes the security and welfare of the people the primary purpose of government, stressing the need to protect citizens participating in legitimate political activities. Agbedi urged the House to invoke Section 88(1) of the Constitution, which empowers the National Assembly to investigate matters within its legislative competence and examine the conduct of public authorities responsible for administering relevant laws. To illustrate the growing concerns, he cited several incidents of political violence recorded in different states. He recalled the disruption of political meetings in Enugu State on September 12, 2026, during which the police reportedly confirmed that two attendees were injured, while one person was allegedly killed. He also cited an attack on APC supporters travelling to a rally in Katsina State on October 28, 2026, which led to the arrest of 14 suspects. In Nasarawa State, Agbedi recalled the attack on an APC rally in Lafia on November 4, 2026, where several people were reportedly injured. He further mentioned a violent incident during a political procession in Asaba, Delta State, on November 7, 2026, in which the police reportedly confirmed that one person was killed and five others injured. The lawmaker warned that continued attacks, intimidation and destruction of property linked to political activities could result in further loss of lives and injuries, while discouraging citizens from participating in the electoral process. He, however, stressed that allegations of responsibility for the incidents must be established through impartial, thorough and evidence-based investigations. The House subsequently constituted an ad hoc committee headed by the Leader of the House, Julius Ihonvbere, to investigate the immediate and remote causes of politically motivated violence and report its findings within three weeks. The committee comprises the House Leader, Minority Leader, chairmen and deputy chairmen of the House Committees on Police Affairs and National Security and Intelligence, as well as two additional members drawn from the committees. NDC demands probe, prosecution Meanwhile, the national leadership of the NDC has condemned the attack on its supporters by suspected political thugs who allegedly invaded its town hall meeting in Oregun, along Kudirat Abiola Way, Ikeja, Lagos. The party demanded the immediate investigation, arrest and prosecution of those responsible, insisting that the incident would not intimidate its members or silence Nigerians. In a statement issued on Thursday and signed by the Spokesperson of the NDC National Campaign Council, Dr Chiogo Constance Ikokwu, the party described the incident as an unacceptable assault on democracy, citizens’ fundamental rights and freedom of political association. It said no political party or group had a monopoly on Nigeria, adding that nobody had the right to deploy violence, intimidation or thuggery to silence opposing voices. The party also called for an end to what it described as the dangerous culture of political violence being witnessed in some states. The statement read: “The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) strongly condemns the violent attack on its supporters in Lagos by suspected political thugs during its town hall meeting today. “We deeply sympathise with anybody injured in the attack and wish them a speedy and full recovery. Our thoughts are with them and their families at this difficult time. “This incident is an unacceptable assault on democracy, citizens’ fundamental rights and the freedom of political association. No political party or group has a monopoly on Nigeria, and no one has the right to use violence, intimidation or thuggery to silence opposing voices. “Nigeria is not a conquered territory, and political participation is not a crime. “We demand an immediate investigation, the arrest and prosecution of those responsible, and an end to the dangerous culture of political violence we are witnessing in some states. “Those who believe they can intimidate Nigerians into silence must understand that democracy belongs to the people, not political thugs and their sponsors.” The party alleged that the attack was part of an attempt to intimidate Nigerians, spread fear and discourage participation in the 2027 elections, but insisted that such efforts would fail. The Lagos meeting was part of the NDC’s campaign activities in support of its presidential candidate, Peter Obi, and governorship candidate, Funsho Doherty. The party urged Nigerians to turn out in large numbers in 2027 to exercise their democratic rights and vote for the Obi/Kwankwaso ticket, describing the call as part of its demand for accountable leadership and a different direction for the country. It maintained that neither the party nor its supporters would be bullied out of exercising their democratic rights. APC-PCC calls for arrests Similarly, the APC Presidential Campaign Council condemned the disruption of the NDC town hall meeting in Lagos and other reported attacks on political gatherings in Edo, Cross River and Gombe states. In a statement issued on Thursday, the Spokesperson of the APC-PCC, Dele Alake, described the attacks as condemnable, regardless of the political parties or individuals affected. “We have observed the recent spate of violent attacks at political gatherings in parts of the country. The reported attacks in Edo, Cross River, and Gombe, and other violence targeted at party supporters and political leaders across party lines are condemnable,” the statement said. On the Lagos incident, the council said: “Our campaign strongly condemns the disruption of today’s scheduled town hall meeting of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in Lagos.” The APC-PCC urged political parties, politicians and their supporters to exercise restraint as campaign activities gathered momentum, warning against actions capable of creating public disorder. It called on security agencies to strengthen their response to political violence and ensure that those responsible were arrested and prosecuted in accordance with the law. “Political parties and candidates are enjoined to campaign on issues that uplift the lives of Nigerians and not to instigate violence at political events,” it added. Lagos APC denies involvement The Lagos State chapter of the APC also condemned the reported attack on NDC members in Ikeja but dismissed allegations linking the ruling party to the incident. The party’s State Publicity Secretary, Seye Oladejo, described the allegation as baseless, challenging the opposition party to present credible evidence to security agencies rather than make public insinuations. In a statement, Oladejo said the allegation was an attempt to drag the APC into an incident without credible evidence linking the party to the disruption. “We consider this allegation not only reckless, baseless and irresponsible but also a desperate attempt to drag Lagos APC into an incident for which the accusers have presented no credible evidence linking the ruling party,” he said. The party noted that the reported incident in Ikeja coincided with the official flag-off of its 2027 general election campaign in Epe, where its leadership, elected officials and stakeholders were mobilised. According to Oladejo, the APC could not have abandoned a major statewide political engagement to interfere with an opposition event. “For the avoidance of doubt, Lagos APC categorically rejects any insinuation of involvement, direct or indirect, in the alleged disruption of the said political gathering. We have neither sponsored, encouraged nor participated in any act capable of undermining the constitutional rights of any political party or group to assemble, deliberate and canvass for political support,” he said. Oladejo maintained that the APC’s position as the governing party in Lagos did not make it responsible for every breach of public order in the state. He described the accusation as “a lazy political reflex that substitutes propaganda for investigation and blame-shifting for accountability.” The APC spokesman urged the NDC to submit any credible evidence linking individuals or groups to the incident to the appropriate security agencies and allow the law to take its course. He also called on the Lagos State Police Command and the Department of State Services (DSS) to investigate the incident and take measures to prevent any breakdown of law and order. Reiterating the party’s commitment to peaceful and issue-based campaigns, Oladejo said political ambition should not be used as a justification for lawlessness and urged political actors to avoid intimidation and disorder as the 2027 elections approach. items.title: Government commits GH¢30bn to New Economy Programme in 2027
items.description: Government is committing GH¢30 billion to its proposed New Economy Programme in 2027, as part of efforts to transform Ghana’s economic structure, expand businesses and create jobs. Presenting the 2027 Budget Statement in Parliament, Finance Minister Dr Ato Forson said the allocation represents 1.5 per cent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and will provide the foundation for the country’s economic transformation agenda. “Mr Speaker, in 2027, we will invest 1.5 per cent of GDP, equivalent to 30 billion Ghana cedis in the New Economy,” he told Parliament. He said the investment will support productive infrastructure, industries and other strategic sectors to expand businesses, increase exports and create employment opportunities. According to Dr Forson, the programme is intended to ensure that economic growth translates into tangible benefits for Ghanaians. “A young Ghanaian will see economic growth reflected in jobs, wages and opportunities. We judge growth by the jobs it creates, the income it raises, and the productive capacity it leaves behind,” he said. The Finance Minister added that every project under the programme will undergo rigorous appraisal and value-for-money assessments to ensure accountability. “Our commitment will be budgeted, authorised and transparently reported,” he assured Parliament. The GH¢30 billion allocation will form part of government’s broader four-year New Economy Programme, which runs from 2027 to 2030.

items.title: Ghana has struggled to sustain a shared economic direction after Dr Nkrumah – Ato Forson
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson says Ghana has struggled to maintain a consistent economic direction since the era of its first President, Osagyefo Dr Kwame Nkrumah, limiting the country’s ability to fully realise its economic potential. According to him, successive governments had pursued development initiatives, but frequent changes in policy direction, economic instability and repeated efforts to recover from crises had disrupted the country’s progress. Presenting the 2027 Budget in Parliament on Thursday, November 12, Dr Forson said Ghana had entered independence with significant natural and human resources and the potential to become an industrial nation. He said Dr Nkrumah recognised that political independence had to be accompanied by economic emancipation and pursued an industrialisation agenda supported by investments in power infrastructure, education and state institutions. “The bare truth is that, Mr Speaker, after Dr Nkrumah, our nation has struggled to sustain a shared economic direction long enough to fulfil its potential,” he said. “Governments have built, businesses have grown, yet these have too often been interrupted intermittently by instability, changes in direction, and the urgent work of repairing another crisis. We have grown, Mr Speaker, but we have not built enough resilience into that growth.” Dr Forson said Ghana’s real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth averaged 5.2 per cent between 1990 and 2025, demonstrating the country’s capacity for economic expansion. However, he said that the average concealed significant volatility, largely driven by the country’s dependence on commodity exports. He explained that periods of rising commodity prices had boosted government revenue and economic confidence, but falling prices and weakened fiscal discipline had often put pressure on the cedi, pushed up inflation and interest rates, and discouraged investment. According to him, Ghana’s dependence on raw commodities, particularly gold, cocoa and oil, had deepened these economic vulnerabilities. “Gold, cocoa, and later oil dominated exports, where extractive industries accounted for about 16% of GDP growth over the last decade. The result is an economy that can post growth figures while leaving too many citizens outside the promise of that growth.” The Finance Minister said the country’s economic growth had also not translated into sufficient employment opportunities for its population. He cited an unemployment rate of about 12.8 per cent in January 2025, despite more than three decades of economic expansion. “Mr Speaker, the best measure of an economy must be an improvement in the quality of life,” he said.

items.title: Ghana to ban commercial rice imports by 2030 under new production plan
items.description: The government plans to prohibit commercial rice imports by the end of 2030 as part of a broader strategy to expand domestic production, create jobs and strengthen the local rice industry. Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson announced the policy while presenting the 2027 Budget to Parliament on Thursday, November 12, 2026. He said the government would also amend public procurement laws to require public institutions to purchase only Ghanaian rice with public funds. The measure will apply to rice and other staple foodstuffs procured for schools, hospitals and other public institutions. Dr Forson said the policy would ensure that public spending supports local farmers while providing a reliable market for their produce. “This will ensure that public spending feeds our children, patients, and other beneficiaries while providing a reliable market for Ghanaian farmers and creating jobs here at home,” he said. As part of the strategy, the government will establish rice development hubs in the Volta Basin, Western Ghana and Northern Ghana. The hubs will bring together irrigation infrastructure, mechanisation, storage facilities, modern mills, packaging and logistics to support production and processing. According to the Finance Minister, the initiative is expected to bring an additional 100,000 hectares under rice cultivation, with targeted yields of between five and six metric tonnes per hectare. He said the hubs would also support about 125,000 jobs. Dr Forson said the rice development hubs would benefit from targeted tax incentives covering investments in irrigation, mechanisation, silos, modern mills, packaging and logistics. “These incentives will lower investment costs, reduce post-harvest losses, and help Ghanaian rice reach consumers at competitive prices,” he said. The government expects the incentives to encourage investment across the rice value chain, from cultivation to processing, storage and distribution. The Finance Minister also announced a new arrangement under which rice import licences will be tied to purchases from verified Ghanaian farmers and millers from 2027. He said the proportion of local rice that importers would be required to purchase would increase as domestic production expands, while import quotas would gradually decline. “Commercial rice imports will be prohibited by end of 2030. That decision will be backed by domestic production, milling, storage, quality assurance, and reliable distribution,” he said. The proposed restrictions are expected to be supported by increased local production and investment in processing and distribution infrastructure. Agriculture remains a significant part of Ghana’s economy, contributing to employment, exports and livelihoods. The government says Ghana spends billions of dollars annually importing food and agricultural products that could be produced locally. The rice policy forms part of the broader effort to increase domestic production, retain more value within the economy and create opportunities for farmers and businesses. Implementation of the rice development hubs, procurement reforms and import-licensing arrangements is expected to begin in 2027.

items.title: Ghana’s 70th anniversary must mark turning point in economic transformation – Ato Forson
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson says Ghana has achieved far less than expected despite gaining independence from colonial rule nearly 70 years ago. He expressed concern that the country has struggled over the years to realise the vision and aspirations of its first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah. According to him, many of the plans and dreams envisioned by Dr Nkrumah remain unfulfilled decades after his demise. “Mr Speaker, in 2027, Ghana will mark 70 years of independence, yet the economic transformation envisioned by Osagyefo Dr Kwame Nkrumah has not been realised. Our economy continues to carry a burden of long-standing structural weakness,” he said. “We depend too heavily on raw materials exports, add little value at home and create few productive jobs for our people,” the finance minister said. Dr Forson said the upcoming 70th anniversary of Ghana’s independence in March 2027 must serve as a turning point for the country. “Our 70th anniversary must mark a decisive turning point,” he said, adding, “the new economy is the government of Ghana’s four-year programme beginning in 2027 to confront this weakness and transform the structure of the Ghanaian economy.” He explained that the 2027 Budget reflects the government’s commitment to making the milestone a new beginning for Ghana through renewed efforts to achieve the country’s development aspirations. He added that the President John Dramani Mahama-led administration is committed to translating that vision into tangible progress for Ghanaians. Dr Ato Forson made these remarks while presenting the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy to Parliament on Thursday, November 12.

items.title: Gov’t to spend $10 billion over 4 years to create a modern Ghanaian economy – Ato Forson
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson has announced that the government plans to invest the equivalent of US$10 billion over four years to build a modern Ghanaian economy, create jobs and improve living standards. Presenting the 2027 Budget and the government’s New Economy agenda to Parliament on Thursday, November 12, the Finance Minister said the programme would run from 2027 to 2030 and focus on eight interconnected pillars aimed at expanding production, strengthening key industries and creating opportunities for Ghanaians. “Over a four-year period, from 2027 to 2030, the government will spend US$10 billion equivalent to create a modern Ghanaian economy for jobs and prosperity,” he said. The eight pillars are macroeconomic stability and affordable finance; commercial agriculture; energy infrastructure; critical minerals value addition; tourism, culture and creative arts; textiles and garments; pharmaceuticals and manufacturing, including biomanufacturing; and the technology economy. According to the Finance Minister, the pillars are designed to work together as one productive system, with each sector supporting the growth of the others. “Affordable finance must reach farmers, manufacturers and exporters. Agriculture must supply food and industrial raw materials, while reliable energy must support a 24-hour economy,” he said. Dr Forson said the government also wanted to ensure that more value was added to Ghana’s natural resources before they were exported. He identified minerals and cocoa as key commodities that should be processed locally to create more jobs and retain a greater share of their value in the country. He said tourism, culture and the creative arts would be developed into stronger sources of business opportunities, employment and foreign exchange by turning Ghana’s heritage and creative talent into commercially successful ventures. On the textiles and garments industry, the Minister said the government intended to expand local production, create jobs and connect Ghanaian skills and businesses to international fashion markets. He also highlighted the importance of building local capacity in pharmaceuticals and biomanufacturing, saying the country must produce more medicines and vaccines to strengthen health security and supply markets across Africa. “Pharmaceuticals and biomanufacturing must produce more medicines and vaccines in Ghana, strengthen health security and supply markets across Africa,” he said. The technology economy, he added, would open up new sources of employment and foreign exchange. He stressed that improved digital connectivity was necessary to ensure that people with the relevant skills could participate in the economy, regardless of where they lived. The Finance Minister said the New Economy Agenda would guide how the government used the fiscal space created by the country’s economic recovery. He explained that the government’s role would be to maintain macroeconomic stability, provide strategic infrastructure, develop bankable projects and create predictable conditions for businesses to operate. The private sector, he said, would be expected to take the lead in investment, innovation and production, as well as the creation of sustainable jobs. “Government support will be transparent, time-bound and linked to verifiable results,” he told Parliament. He added that the government would protect the gains made in the economic recovery through fiscal discipline, greater accountability and diligence, while pursuing faster economic growth and higher employment. The Finance Minister said the success of the programme would not be judged only by the amount of money spent or the number of projects undertaken. Instead, the government would measure its impact by the jobs created, improvements in people’s quality of life and the pace of development in communities across the country. He urged Ghanaians to support the government’s vision for the country’s economic future, arguing that the recovery presented an opportunity to make long-term investments rather than repeat past mistakes. “I call on Ghanaians to make a defining national choice about the future we want to build. We can spend the recovery as though history has taught us nothing, or invest in it,” he said.

items.title: Join Rainbow Coalition or leave, Fubara warns supporters
items.description: Rivers State Governor, Siminalayi Fubara, has warned his supporters who are unwilling to align with the Rainbow Coalition to leave, insisting that his decision to return to his political camp is final. Fubara gave the warning on Thursday during the inauguration of the Rivers State All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council, Rainbow Coalition, in Port Harcourt. Addressing party members and supporters, the governor urged those whose names were not included in the campaign council list not to feel aggrieved, explaining that there were still sub-committees to be constituted and that the list could be updated. He, however, warned against double-dealing, insisting that those claiming to support him must demonstrate genuine commitment to the coalition. “We still have sub-committees. The list can also be updated so you don’t have any problems to worry about. The most important thing is to work with your heart sincerely. “Don’t openly say you’re with me and behold you’re doing a different thing. I’m here, and I say it boldly anywhere, any day. And anybody who says he is not with me, gently go your way,” he said. Acknowledging that some of his supporters might find it difficult to accept the new political direction, Fubara urged them to put the past behind them and embrace the future. “Don’t go behind and say this is Fubara, no, no, no. I have said it. It might be difficult but we have gone past that. We are looking at the future and what God holds for us,” he added. The governor charged members of the campaign council to work together to achieve their political objectives, expressing confidence that the coalition would record more votes in the forthcoming elections than it secured in 2023. “Nothing is impossible. Provided it’s something that has to do with life, it is possible if we take it as a serious responsibility, a serious task that must be achieved, we will come out with a stronger vote than what we did in 2023. “It is only for us to say yes, we want to do it. And I am very sure that with the strategy of these forthcoming elections we are going to come out with good results better than what we had before,” he said. Fubara also thanked the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, and other political leaders for their efforts in establishing the campaign council. Earlier, Wike, who inaugurated the council, announced plans to establish similar campaign structures across the 23 local government areas of Rivers State. He said the coalition would abandon conventional campaign rallies in favour of direct engagement with residents through community gatherings, family meetings and age-grade associations. “We are going away from that ceremonial campaign style. When we are going to Gokana today, we just stay in one field and begin to talk to those we already know. “It is going to be different. This time around we are going round to communities, to family meetings, to age-grade meetings and other informal sects to talk to them, not necessarily those we meet with every day. “You and I meet every day; then tomorrow again we gather in one place, we say we are holding a rally. We must depart from that,” Wike said. The minister commended Fubara for attending the inauguration and other engagements of the council despite his busy schedule. Wike, who is also the National Leader of the PDP/Rainbow Coalition, said members of the campaign council were selected based on their capacity to participate in its activities and deliver results. He urged them to mobilise support for APC and Rainbow Coalition candidates in the 2027 presidential, governorship, National Assembly and State House of Assembly elections. He further disclosed that local government campaign councils would soon be inaugurated to strengthen the coalition’s grassroots mobilisation. Background The development is the latest chapter in the prolonged political crisis between Fubara and Wike, who governed Rivers State from 2015 to 2023 and supported Fubara’s emergence as his successor. Their disagreement, which became public in October 2023, centred on control of the state’s political structures and influence over the Rivers State House of Assembly. The crisis split lawmakers into opposing camps and triggered repeated impeachment moves against Fubara. The dispute escalated in March 2025 when President Bola Tinubu declared a state of emergency in Rivers State, resulting in the suspension of the governor, his deputy and members of the State House of Assembly for six months. The elected officials returned to office in September 2025 following the expiration of the emergency rule. Reconciliation efforts gathered momentum in 2026 after Wike announced an end to the feud and a reconciliation committee was constituted to engage Fubara and his supporters. The Rainbow Coalition, led by Wike, comprises political actors from different parties, including the APC and the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), working towards Tinubu’s re-election bid in 2027. Fubara subsequently declared support for the coalition and endorsed Kingsley Chinda as his preferred successor in the 2027 Rivers governorship election. He also withdrew from the APC governorship contest, citing the need to promote peace and unity in the state. items.title: “Black Stars clean sheet against Somalia is a big relief” – Jonas Adjetey
items.description: Jonas Adjetey has expressed his delight after scoring his first goal for the Black Stars in Ghana’s 2-0 victory over Somalia in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers. The defender found the net as Ghana secured their first victory since consecutive defeats to Côte d’Ivoire and The Gambia. The result provided a positive start for interim coach Kim Lars Björkegren, who took charge following the dismissal of Carlos Queiroz. For Adjetey, however, the occasion carried additional significance as he finally opened his scoring account for the senior national team. “It feels amazing to score my first goal. I have been waiting for this moment for some time now. My teammates have been very supportive and I am glad that I had such an opportunity,” he said after the match. The defender also expressed satisfaction with Ghana’s defensive performance, particularly the clean sheet after conceding four goals across their previous two qualifying matches. Adjetey insisted the goals conceded in those games were not the responsibility of any individual player but acknowledged the need for collective improvement. “Unfortunately, we did our best in previous games but it did not go our way. “The goals we conceded in the first two games had nothing to do with any individual or anything like that, but we have corrected our mistakes and it was good to keep a clean sheet today,” he added. The Black Stars will look to maintain their defensive improvement when they face Somalia again on Monday.

items.title: De Miguel death made me thank God over Zidane headbutt — Materazzi
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Former Italy defender Marco Materazzi says the death of Spanish striker Jesus de Miguel after an on-field collision made him reflect on the headbutt he suffered from Zinedine Zidane in the 2006 World Cup final. Materazzi said the incident, one of football’s most infamous World Cup moments, still troubled him 20 years later. He told Italian newspaper La Gazzetta dello Sport that De Miguel’s death made him grateful he had escaped serious injury. “The death of Jesus de Miguel made me thank God that nothing had happened to me,” Materazzi said in an interview published on Thursday. De Miguel, a Tenerife striker, died after colliding with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a Segunda Division match earlier this month. Zidane, then captain of France, was sent off for headbutting Materazzi in the chest during the 2006 final, which Italy won on penalties. Zidane, now France coach, said last month he was not proud of the headbutt but did not regret it. Materazzi said he and Zidane appeared to put the episode behind them when they met before a match in 2010, although Zidane later disputed Materazzi’s account of the encounter. “When he saw me, he hesitated a little, he even turned to walk back,” Materazzi said. “But I approached him and shook his hand: ‘I’m glad we’re meeting here, where nobody can see us.’ “He replied: ‘Don’t worry, these things happen, it’s all in the past.’ It’s a shame he later denied everything, saying he thought I was a fan.” France are scheduled to play Italy in the Nations League later on Thursday. items.title: Government wants natural wealth to deliver jobs and improved livelihoods – Ato Forson
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson has called for a deliberate shift towards using Ghana’s natural and economic resources to generate employment, expand local industries and improve the living standards of citizens. Presenting the 2027 Budget to Parliament on Thursday, November 12, 2026, he said the country must ensure that its resources deliver measurable economic benefits rather than remain untapped or contribute little to national development. “Every cedi of that space must answer a national question: What jobs will it create? What import will it replace? What export will it generate? And what lasting value will it leave behind?” he said. Dr Forson said the government’s New Economy programme was designed to redirect resources towards productive sectors, strengthen domestic production and ensure that economic recovery translates into sustainable prosperity. He said the framework would prioritise investments in agriculture, manufacturing, infrastructure, energy and critical minerals, with a focus on value addition, job creation and expanding opportunities for local businesses. The Finance Minister stressed that the benefits of economic stability must be felt by ordinary Ghanaians through decent employment, rising incomes and improved livelihoods. “Our natural and economic wealth must translate into improved living conditions, decent jobs and opportunities for all,” he said.

items.title: Government targets 8% GDP growth, unemployment below 8% by 2030
items.description: The government is targeting real gross domestic product (GDP) growth of about 8 per cent and an unemployment rate below 8 per cent by 2030 under its New Economy programme. Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson announced the targets during the presentation of the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy to Parliament on Thursday, November 12, 2026. He said the government was also seeking to establish a credible path towards securing an investment-grade sovereign credit rating. “By 2030, we are targeting real GDP growth of about 8%, unemployment below 8%, and a credible path to an investment-grade sovereign credit rating,” he said. Dr Forson stressed that an investment-grade rating could not be secured through declarations but would depend on sustained economic performance. “Investment grade sovereign rating cannot be conferred in a speech. It must be earned through sustained performance,” he said. He announced plans to publish an annual investment-grade readiness report assessing the country’s progress across key economic and institutional indicators. The report will cover fiscal performance, debt affordability, reserve accumulation, monetary credibility, financial sector strength, institutional quality and economic diversification. The Finance Minister identified the sustainability of macroeconomic stability and access to affordable financing as the first pillar of the New Economy programme. He said the government intended to maintain a positive primary surplus of at least 0.5 per cent of GDP from 2027, while keeping public debt consistent with a 45 per cent of GDP target. “From 2027, we will maintain a positive primary surplus of at least 0.5% of GDP. We will keep public debt consistent with 45% of GDP. We will preserve single-digit inflation and strengthen our external buffers,” he said. The government has completed its International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme and says it is now focusing on economic transformation through the New Economy plan. The programme identifies commercial agriculture, energy, critical minerals, textiles and garments, tourism, and pharmaceuticals as priority sectors for development.

items.title: Réformer le secteur minier en période de transition politique : pourquoi les choix de l'État changent-ils au Burkina Faso ?
items.description: SOURA Sibiri¹ et SAIDOU Abdoul Karim² ¹ Centre national de la recherche scientifique et technologique (CNRST), Burkina Faso ² Université Thomas Sankara, Burkina Faso Auteur correspondant : SOURA Sibiri, Email : sibirisoura@cnrst Introduction Pourquoi deux régimes de transition peuvent-ils décider de réformer le même secteur stratégique sans nécessairement poursuivre les mêmes objectifs ni privilégier les mêmes moyens ? Cette question se pose particulièrement dans le secteur minier burkinabè. L'or occupe désormais une place majeure dans l'économie nationale. En 2021, le secteur minier représentait 79,02 % des recettes d'exportation du pays, 19,25 % des recettes totales de l'État et 14,34 % du produit intérieur brut. Il contribue également aux ressources des collectivités locales et à l'activité de nombreuses entreprises nationales. Cette importance économique ne suffit pourtant pas à expliquer pourquoi le secteur minier devient un chantier majeur de réforme dans les périodes de transition politique. Les mines ont également une forte portée symbolique. La manière dont l'État organise leur exploitation, collecte les ressources qui en sont issues ou associe les acteurs nationaux peut être utilisée par les gouvernants pour traduire leur conception du changement politique et économique. L'article montre ainsi que le secteur minier a constitué une priorité aussi bien pour la transition conduite par Michel Kafando en 2015 que pour celle dirigée par le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré depuis 2022, mais avec des orientations différentes. Les périodes de transition offrent en effet des circonstances particulières pour engager des réformes. Elles peuvent ouvrir un moment au cours duquel des problèmes déjà connus, des solutions disponibles et une volonté politique de changement se rencontrent plus facilement (Kingdon, 2014). Mais une même volonté de réforme peut se traduire par des choix différents. Pour comprendre ces différences, l'étude s'intéresse aux moyens concrets utilisés par l'État pour agir : lois, taxes, fonds publics, agences, règles d'emploi, mécanismes de participation ou encore création d'entreprises publiques. Les spécialistes des politiques publiques les appellent des « instruments d'action publique ». Ces instruments ne sont pas de simples outils techniques : leur choix renseigne aussi sur la manière dont les gouvernants conçoivent le rôle de l'État et ses relations avec les entreprises et la société (Lascoumes et Le Galès, 2004). L'étude pose donc une question centrale : comment les logiques propres aux différents régimes de transition influencent-elles le choix des moyens utilisés pour réformer le secteur minier au Burkina Faso ? Méthodologie L'étude s'est appuyée sur une recherche documentaire et des entretiens réalisés dans le cadre d'une recherche doctorale. Une quinzaine d'acteurs ont été interrogés entre 2022 et 2023. Ils provenaient du monde politico-administratif, des sociétés minières, de la société civile et du milieu de l'expertise. Les chercheurs ont également analysé des discours, des rapports, des documents officiels ainsi que des travaux consacrés aux politiques minières, aux régimes de transition et aux moyens utilisés par l'État pour conduire ses politiques. Cette démarche comparative a permis d'examiner les réformes engagées sous deux régimes de transition : celui de Michel Kafando en 2015 et celui du capitaine Ibrahim Traoré. L'objectif n'était pas seulement d'identifier les mesures adoptées, mais de comprendre pourquoi certains moyens avaient été privilégiés et ce qu'ils révélaient des orientations de chacun des deux régimes. Résultats 1. Les périodes de transition placent plus facilement les mines au cœur des réformes Le premier résultat montre que les périodes de transition ont constitué, dans les deux cas étudiés, des moments particulièrement favorables aux changements dans le secteur minier. Cela tient d'abord au poids économique des mines. Avec l'essor de l'exploitation industrielle de l'or depuis 2008, le secteur est devenu une source majeure d'exportations, de recettes publiques et d'activités économiques. L'exploitation artisanale constitue également une source de revenus pour environ 1,2 million de personnes. Mais les auteurs montrent que l'importance économique du secteur n'explique pas tout. Les mines représentent également un domaine dans lequel les régimes de transition peuvent rendre visible leur volonté de changement. En 2015, les attentes portaient notamment sur la transparence et la gestion du secteur. Des organisations de la société civile ayant participé aux mobilisations de 2014 défendaient depuis plusieurs années une gouvernance plus transparente et participative. La réforme minière constituait donc l'un des domaines dans lesquels la transition pouvait traduire cette volonté de changement en mesures concrètes. Sous le régime du capitaine Traoré, la réforme du secteur minier prend une autre signification. Le contrôle national des ressources occupe une place importante dans les orientations du régime. Les réformes minières deviennent ainsi l'un des moyens de renforcer la présence de l'État et des acteurs nationaux dans l'exploitation, la transformation et la commercialisation des ressources minières. Dans les deux périodes, le secteur minier offre donc une possibilité de matérialiser le changement politique. Cependant, ce que signifie « changer » n'est pas exactement la même chose d'un régime à l'autre. 2. En 2015, les réformes privilégient la réglementation, la transparence et le développement local Sous la transition Kafando, la réforme du Code minier de 2015 a introduit plusieurs changements dans la manière d'organiser le secteur. Certains concernent directement l'encadrement des activités minières. Les règles relatives aux permis de recherche et d'exploitation ont été revues et l'Agence nationale d'encadrement des exploitations minières artisanales et semi-mécanisées (ANEEMAS) a été créée. Sa mission consistait notamment à mieux encadrer l'exploitation artisanale, suivre les circuits de commercialisation, réduire l'informalité et prendre en compte la restauration des sites dégradés. La réforme a également créé plusieurs fonds. Le Fonds minier de développement local devait notamment permettre aux ressources provenant du secteur minier de participer au financement du développement des collectivités. D'autres fonds étaient consacrés à la recherche géologique et minière, à la réhabilitation des mines après leur fermeture ou encore à la sécurisation et à la restauration des sites d'exploitation artisanale. La fiscalité a elle aussi été modifiée. Le taux de l'impôt sur les bénéfices des sociétés minières, auparavant fixé à 17,5 %, a été aligné sur le taux de droit commun de 27,5 %. À ces mesures réglementaires et économiques s'ajoutaient des outils mettant davantage l'accent sur la transparence et la participation. Le régime Kafando a notamment réaffirmé l'adhésion du Burkina Faso à l'Initiative pour la transparence dans les industries extractives (ITIE) ainsi qu'au Processus de Kimberley. Pris séparément, une taxe, un fonds ou une agence peuvent paraître essentiellement techniques. Mais considérés ensemble, ces choix révèlent une orientation plus générale. Dans l'analyse de Soura et Saidou, la réforme de 2015 s'inscrivait dans une volonté de renforcer la transparence, la redevabilité et la gouvernance démocratique. C'est précisément pourquoi les moyens choisis par un gouvernement ne sont jamais totalement neutres : ils traduisent aussi une certaine manière d'organiser les relations entre l'État, les entreprises et la société (Lascoumes et Le Galès, 2004). 3. Sous le régime Traoré, les réformes renforcent la présence de l'État et la participation nationale Les réformes engagées à partir de 2023 empruntent une autre direction. Elles mettent davantage l'accent sur le rôle de l'État, la participation des acteurs nationaux et la maîtrise d'une partie plus importante de la chaîne de valeur minière. Un décret adopté en 2023 a par exemple établi une nomenclature des emplois et des quotas afin de renforcer la préférence nationale dans l'emploi minier. La même période voit la création de la Société nationale des substances précieuses (SONASP), chargée notamment de la production, de la transformation et de la commercialisation de produits miniers et de substances précieuses. La transformation locale prend également une place plus importante. Le projet de raffinerie d'or est conçu sous la forme d'une société d'économie mixte dont la SONASP doit détenir 51 % du capital. L'étude précise que cette orientation ne consiste pas à retirer systématiquement la production aux entreprises étrangères, mais à renforcer le rôle de l'État et des investisseurs nationaux dans le secteur. Cette logique se retrouve dans les réformes sur le contenu local. Celles-ci cherchent notamment à développer les capacités nationales dans la fourniture de biens et de services aux sociétés minières, à favoriser le transfert de technologies et à renforcer la présence de travailleurs et d'investisseurs nationaux dans la chaîne de valeur. Le nouveau Code minier adopté le 18 juillet 2024 poursuit cette orientation. Il prévoit notamment la participation des sociétés minières à la constitution d'une réserve nationale d'or, un droit de préemption de l'État sur la commercialisation de certaines substances minérales et une augmentation de la participation gratuite de l'État au capital des sociétés minières, qui passe de 10 à 15 %. Ces différents changements traduisent, selon l'étude, une évolution du rôle économique de l'État. Celui-ci ne se limite plus à fixer les règles et à contrôler leur respect : il cherche davantage à intervenir directement dans certaines étapes de la production, de la transformation et de la commercialisation. Cette évolution n'implique cependant pas la disparition de tous les instruments antérieurs. L'article souligne notamment que les engagements pris en matière de transparence, en particulier vis-à-vis de l'ITIE, n'ont pas été supprimés. 4. Les mêmes mines, mais des objectifs politiques différents La comparaison permet finalement de comprendre un résultat essentiel : ce n'est pas seulement le type d'outil utilisé qui différencie les deux régimes, mais surtout l'objectif auquel cet outil est associé. Sous la transition Kafando, les auteurs identifient une orientation principalement centrée sur la démocratie, la transparence, la redevabilité et la volonté de marquer une rupture avec les pratiques antérieures. Les organisations de la société civile et plusieurs acteurs ayant longtemps défendu des réformes de gouvernance ont trouvé dans la transition de 2014-2015 une occasion de faire avancer des changements sur lesquels ils travaillaient déjà. Le caractère temporaire de la transition renforçait cette dynamique. Certains acteurs considéraient que l'occasion de réformer pouvait se refermer avec la fin de la période transitionnelle. Il fallait donc utiliser rapidement ce moment pour faire adopter certaines réformes, notamment dans un secteur aussi stratégique que les mines. Cette situation illustre bien l'idée selon laquelle certaines périodes politiques peuvent ouvrir une occasion particulière de changement (Kingdon, 2014). Sous le régime Traoré, l'orientation mise en évidence par l'article est différente. Les réformes sont principalement reliées à la souveraineté sur les ressources, au renforcement de la participation nationale et au contexte sécuritaire. Une partie des ressources du Fonds minier de développement local a ainsi été orientée vers le Fonds de soutien patriotique, destiné à contribuer au financement de l'effort de guerre. Le Code minier de 2024 confirme cette articulation. Le Fonds minier de développement prend désormais en compte, en plus des plans communaux de développement, des projets de développement endogène et le Fonds de soutien patriotique. Les taux plafonds de certaines redevances minières ont également été relevés de 5 à 7 %, en fonction du prix de l'or. L'étude aboutit ainsi à une conclusion importante : les choix opérés dans le secteur minier reposent à la fois sur des idées et sur des préoccupations très concrètes. En 2015, la réforme est étroitement liée aux attentes de renouvellement de la gouvernance après la fin du régime Compaoré. Sous le régime Traoré, la souveraineté économique et les impératifs liés à la crise sécuritaire pèsent davantage sur l'orientation des réformes. Cela ne signifie pas que les deux régimes utilisent des catégories de moyens totalement opposées. Ils ont tous deux recours à des lois, à des fonds, à des agences ou à des mesures fiscales. La différence se trouve surtout dans ce qu'ils cherchent à obtenir à travers ces moyens. C'est précisément ce qui donne tout son intérêt à l'étude des instruments d'action publique : derrière une taxe, une agence, un fonds ou une nouvelle règle se trouve aussi une certaine conception du rôle que l'État entend jouer dans le secteur minier. Conclusion L'étude montre que les périodes de transition ne modifient pas seulement les institutions politiques. Elles peuvent également accélérer les transformations de politiques économiques aussi importantes que la politique minière. Au Burkina Faso, les transitions Kafando et Traoré ont toutes deux fait des mines un domaine important de réforme, mais les choix opérés répondent à des orientations différentes. En 2015, l'accent est davantage mis sur la transparence, la gouvernance et la participation ; sous le régime Traoré, les réformes mettent davantage l'accent sur la souveraineté sur les ressources, la participation nationale, le renforcement du rôle économique de l'État et les impératifs liés à la crise sécuritaire. Le principal enseignement est donc simple : les moyens choisis par l'État pour agir ne sont jamais de simples détails techniques. Ils renseignent aussi sur les objectifs poursuivis par les gouvernants et sur la place qu'ils souhaitent donner à l'État dans l'économie. Ce document de vulgarisation est tiré de l'article scientifique : SOURA, Sibiri et SAIDOU, Abdoul Karim (2025), « Régimes de transition et action publique : le cas de la politique minière au Burkina Faso », Politique africaine, n° 180, 2025/4, pp. 197-214. Références bibliographiques KINGDON, John W. (2014), Agendas, Alternatives, and Public Policies, Harlow, Pearson. LASCOUMES, Pierre et LE GALÈS, Patrick (dir.) (2004), Gouverner par les instruments, Paris, Presses de Sciences Po. SOURA, Sibiri et SAIDOU, Abdoul Karim (2025), « Régimes de transition et action publique : le cas de la politique minière au Burkina Faso », Politique africaine, n° 180, 2025/4, pp. 197-214.

items.title: SmartPensions targets informal sector workers as People’s Pension Trust, Pan-African launch retirement scheme
items.description: People’s Pension Trust Ghana Limited and Pan-African Savings and Loans have launched SmartPensions, a retirement savings initiative aimed at extending pension coverage to informal sector workers and making retirement planning more accessible to Ghanaians. The initiative, launched at Madina market in Accra, is designed to enable traders, artisans, drivers, entrepreneurs and other self-employed individuals to build retirement savings through flexible daily, weekly and monthly contributions. The partnership seeks to address the retirement planning gap among workers outside the formal employment sector, many of whom lack structured arrangements to secure their financial future after years of economic activity. Chief Executive Officer of People’s Pension Trust, Ibrahim Issaka, said the initiative was designed to address the longstanding perception that pension savings are primarily for people in formal employment. “The market trader, the entrepreneur, the artisan and the self-employed person also deserve a comfortable and dignified retirement,” he said. He said the partnership with Pan-African Savings and Loans would help bring pension services closer to people in their workplaces and communities. Managing Director of Pan-African Savings and Loans, Jacqueline Dufie Mpare, said the initiative also provides an opportunity for informal sector workers to build financial independence rather than depend on their children for support during retirement. She urged traders and market women to begin saving with whatever they could afford, noting that consistency was more important than the size of their initial contributions. “Do not wait until you have plenty before you begin; whatever you can spare today will be worth more to you tomorrow,” she said. Managing Director of EDC Investments Limited, Paul Mante, said retirement planning must go beyond setting money aside, emphasising the importance of investing contributions to support long-term wealth creation. “Earning money and building wealth are two different things. A person can work for thirty years and still retire with nothing. Hard work alone is not a financial plan,” he said. Mr Mante explained that SmartPensions provides workers with irregular incomes the opportunity to contribute towards retirement through flexible daily, weekly and monthly payment arrangements. He noted that contributions are invested in accordance with applicable pension regulations and investment guidelines, with the objective of growing members’ retirement savings. “Saving alone is not enough. Your money must be invested so that it can grow,” he stressed. The initiative is part of efforts by the three institutions to deepen financial inclusion and extend structured retirement savings opportunities to workers who have traditionally been underserved by formal pension arrangements.

items.title: 3 terrorists killed, 2 civilians dead as attack on Mastung post repelled: state media
items.description: Security forces killed three terrorists on the N-25 highway in Balochistan’s Mastung district while repelling an attack on Kandawa Post, state broadcaster Radio Pakistan reported on Thursday, citing police. According to a spokesperson for Balochistan Police, terrorists belonging to Fitna al Hindustan attempted a “cowardly attack at Kandawa Post on National Highway N-25 using an explosives-laden vehicle”. The state has designated Balochistan-based terrorist groups as Fitna al-Hindustan to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. Security forces repulsed the attack through timely and effective action, the police statement said. However, two civilians lost their lives in the incident, while at least 13 others were injured, according to a list of names in the police statement. Three Frontier Corps personnel were also injured in the incident, the statement added. “The explosion caused damage to nearby houses and a mosque.” In the ensuing retaliatory operation, three terrorists were killed, the police said. The injured people were taken to medical centres for treatment. “The attack demonstrates that these terrorists have no connection with the people of Balochistan,” the police stressed. “Operations against elements seeking to undermine peace, development, and prosperity in Balochistan will continue, and the protection of the lives and property of the people will be ensured under all circumstances,” it affirmed. Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years, prompting security forces to intensify counter-terrorism operations. Earlier this month, a soldier was martyred and 17 terrorists were killed in two intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan’s Kachhi and Kharan districts, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said. In early October, security forces killed five terrorists belonging to Fitna al-Hindustan in Mastung, Pakistan TV reported. Pakistan witnessed a significant improvement in several key security indicators during October , with terrorist attacks declining by 37 per cent compared with September, according to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). Balochistan recorded one of the most significant improvements, with terrorist attacks declining by 46pc, from 132 in September to 71 in October.

items.title: “Black Stars must be more clinical after Somalia victory” – Interim Coach, Kim Lars Björkegren
items.description: Interim Black Stars coach Kim Lars Björkegren believes Ghana must improve their speed of play and finishing despite opening his tenure with a 2-0 victory over Somalia. The Swedish coach guided the Black Stars to victory in their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying encounter at the Essipong Sports Stadium in Takoradi on Thursday. However, Björkegren admitted his side lacked intensity during the first half, with the conditions also making it difficult for the players. “We were struggling a little bit. I don’t know if the heat was too much, but the intensity was a bit low in the first half,” he said. The coach was more satisfied with Ghana’s performance after the break, when the team raised their energy levels and created several opportunities. Despite the improved display, he believes there is room for progress, particularly in how quickly his players move the ball. “I think we can play the ball a bit faster than we did, especially in the first half. But I respect the effort because the heat makes it not easy to play,” he said. Björkegren also highlighted Ghana’s inability to convert all their chances as another area requiring attention. “Of course, we can improve on many aspects from today’s game, especially in terms of taking our chances,” he added. The interim coach is optimistic Ghana can deliver another positive performance in Monday’s return encounter. He believes the first meeting will provide his technical team with a better understanding of Somalia ahead of the next game. “We did not have that much information about Somalia, and the good thing now is that after playing the first match, we know a bit more about them. “I absolutely think we can do a second good game as well,” he said.

items.title: Ghana has regained stability, confidence and breathing space – Ato Forson
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson says Ghana has made significant economic gains and emerged from what he describes as the most painful economic crisis in the country’s history. He said economic stability had returned, confidence was being restored, and Ghanaians could now “breathe again” after a difficult period. Speaking during the presentation of the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy to Parliament, Dr Ato Forson said the country had reached a critical point where decisions taken by government would determine the future of millions of Ghanaians. He stressed that the breathing space created by the return of economic stability must be used to make decisions that would improve livelihoods and create opportunities for people across the country. “Ghana has made significant gains and has emerged from the most painful economic crisis in our history. Stability has returned, confidence is back, and Ghanaians can breathe again,” he said. The Finance Minister said the next phase of the country’s economic journey must focus on translating the gains into tangible improvements in the lives of citizens. He identified young graduates seeking employment, farmers looking for reliable markets for their produce and market women whose working capital had been eroded by inflation among those whose circumstances needed to improve. He also highlighted pensioners whose life savings, he said, had been wiped out overnight by the debt restructuring exercise, as well as entrepreneurs who had the ambition to build businesses but lacked access to affordable long-term financing. According to him, the choices made at this stage must respond to the needs of these groups and ensure that the benefits of economic recovery extend beyond improved economic indicators. Dr Ato Forson said the decisions would have far-reaching consequences for millions of Ghanaians, making it important for government to use the opportunity created by renewed stability to shape a more secure economic future. He indicated that the 2027 Budget would set out the policy direction for the next phase of the country’s economic management.

items.title: Ghana has overcome the worst and most painful economic crisis in its history – Finance Minister
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson says Ghana has made significant progress in recovering from what he describes as “the worst economic crisis in the country’s history.” He said the economy had regained stability and investor and public confidence had returned, pointing to the progress made since the government began implementing measures to address the economic challenges. Dr Forson made the remarks while presenting the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy in Parliament on Thursday, November 12, 2026, as the government outlined its next phase of economic management under the proposed US$10 billion ‘New Economy’ programme. “Ghana has made significant gains and has emerged from the worst and the most painful economic crisis in our history. Stability has been achieved, and confidence is back,” he stated. The four-year initiative, covering 2027 to 2030, is expected to channel investments into agriculture, manufacturing, infrastructure, energy, critical minerals, tourism and other strategic sectors to expand domestic production, promote value addition and create employment.
