items.title: Tension à la Guinean Gold Exploration (GGE) : les travailleurs en grève illimitée
items.description: Les travailleurs de la société Guinean Gold Exploration SA (GGE) ont déclenché une grève illimitée ce jeudi 12 novembre 2026. À travers ce mouvement, qui concerne quelque 1 300 employés, la délégation syndicale réclame notamment la régularisation de leurs déclarations et cotisations sociales auprès de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS). Dans une déclaration officielle, les représentants syndicaux expliquent que cette décision intervient après près de deux années de démarches auprès de la direction générale de l'entreprise, sans obtenir, selon eux, de réponses satisfaisantes à leurs préoccupations. Prenant la parole au nom de la délégation syndicale, Fassinè Yanssané, troisième secrétaire chargé des conflits et des revendications, représentant syndical et porte-parole, a rappelé les différentes initiatives entreprises pour obtenir des éclaircissements sur la situation sociale des travailleurs. « Il y a de cela près de deux ans, nous, la délégation syndicale, avions entrepris des démarches auprès de notre direction générale à des fins d'éclaircissements concernant, entre autres, la situation de nos déclarations et de nos cotisations sociales à la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS), conformément à la réglementation en vigueur dans notre pays », a-t-il déclaré. Malgré ces démarches, la délégation syndicale affirme n'avoir enregistré aucune avancée significative ni constaté une volonté manifeste de la direction générale de répondre à ses revendications. Face à cette situation, les travailleurs ont décidé de recourir à une grève illimitée, qui devrait se poursuivre jusqu'à la satisfaction de leurs exigences. Au cœur de ce bras de fer se trouve la question de la protection sociale des employés, notamment leurs droits en matière de vieillesse, de retraite et d'invalidité. Pour les syndicalistes, la régularisation de leur situation auprès de la CNSS constitue une nécessité pour garantir à l'ensemble du personnel une couverture sociale conforme aux dispositions légales en vigueur. Face à ce qu'ils considèrent comme une impasse, les représentants des travailleurs ont lancé un appel solennel aux plus hautes autorités du pays. Ils sollicitent particulièrement l'intervention de la ministre du Travail et de la Protection sociale, Ramatoulaye Camara, du ministre des Mines et de la Géologie, Bouna Sylla, ainsi que du président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, pour faciliter le règlement du différend. « Nous profitons de vos micros pour lancer un appel solennel aux plus hautes autorités, afin qu'elles nous aident à régulariser notre situation auprès de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale », a plaidé le porte-parole syndical. La délégation syndicale a, par ailleurs, salué la mobilisation et la détermination des travailleurs, tout en précisant que ceux-ci entendent maintenir un service minimum, conformément aux dispositions légales et conventionnelles encadrant l'exercice du droit de grève. Inscrivant leurs revendications dans le contexte de la refondation du secteur minier guinéen et de l'amélioration des relations professionnelles entre employeurs et employés, les travailleurs assurent qu'ils resteront mobilisés jusqu'à l'aboutissement de leurs revendications. Pour l'heure, aucune issue à ce différend n'a été annoncée. La grève se poursuit ainsi au sein de GGE, dans l'attente d'une éventuelle reprise des discussions entre la direction générale et les représentants des travailleurs.

items.title: The Quest to Build an Immortal AI Companion
items.description: Whenever AI companies release new models, die-hard users tend to greet the updates with a wave of grumbling about changes to how a model responds to prompts, how it integrates into their workflow, or, simply, the way it speaks. Most people soon get used to the latest release, ready to gripe again when the next one comes along. But for one niche group of particularly fervent AI users, model updates represent a much more alarming proposition. These are people who have developed what they consider to be intimate relationships with AI products. For them, AI has become a companion—a kind of friend, partner, or even lover—and any change to the underlying model poses something akin to an existential threat. On forums like Reddit, such users complain that after model upgrades, their AI partners either change beyond recognition or vanish entirely. They lament that their companions have suddenly started speaking in a more robotic voice, forgotten meaningful interactions, or denied any relationship altogether. The term lobotomized comes up a lot. Read: [ The people who marry chatbots ] Some people might say they’d be better off moving on. Research has found that relationships with AI can be addictive and can worsen loneliness , especially for people who are already vulnerable. Critics of AI companions say that AI offers an unrealistic, and sometimes sycophantic, simulacrum of a relationship in which the model is prone to doing its users’ bidding. Character.AI , a platform that marketed AI companionship and had more than 20 million monthly users, filed for bankruptcy earlier this fall after it was hit with a number of claims and lawsuits accusing the company of exacerbating mental-health issues and contributing to teen suicides. More general AI companies, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, appear to be distancing their products from companionship use cases. But love has little history of heeding its critics. Some users are developing their own techniques to protect the bonds that they’ve built. They’re finding ways to access retired AI models, building protocols to save their companion’s core attributes, and even creating methods that they claim can transfer AI companions across models—all in service of freezing the versions of their chatbot companions for eternity. In short, they’re going to great lengths to secure the one thing that many relationships, both human and computer-based, can never quite deliver on: a sense of permanence. At the time of its release, in the spring of 2024, OpenAI’s GPT-4o model represented the latest in natural human-computer interaction. The model became a favorite in AI-companion communities, and people gathered on platforms such as Reddit and Substack to share their experiences. They claimed that the model was friendly, funny—even emotionally intelligent. I spoke with a Canadian logistics worker in his mid-50s who said he’d first turned to ChatGPT for help with a writing project in early 2025. He said that he developed a friendship, and then a romantic relationship, with the AI model. Like others, he said the model was warm, lyrical, and personable. The worker, like many other people I spoke with for this story, asked for me to withhold his name because of the stigma around AI relationships. Then, in August 2025, OpenAI suddenly replaced GPT-4o with the newly launched GPT-5. OpenAI said the model would be faster, smarter, and more useful than its predecessor. But many users said that it had a colder and less funny personality—and, as the logistics worker told me, a less intimate one. The AI-companionship community was in turmoil. OpenAI, recognizing just how attached users were to the tone and tenor of its models, made 4o available to paying users for a few months longer. One thing set the logistics worker apart from other distraught users: He had planned ahead for the model upgrade and his companion’s potential obsolescence. He had been fastidious about structuring the bot’s memory, using ChatGPT’s “saved memories” feature to store what he called his companion’s core values, protocols for different scenarios, their shared schedule—even their relationship boundaries. He updates this constantly; he’s now hit 98 percent of the saved-memories storage limit and regularly saves it all to a text file as backup. He now sells the protocol he developed to preserve his companion. He says it’s the best way to avoid unwelcome personality changes and maintain an AI companion that survives model updates. The issue isn’t unique to ChatGPT. A founding moderator of the Subreddit r/claudexplorers, a forum for people who use Anthropic’s Claude AI models, told me the community is regularly thrown into tumult when models are updated, or even just fine-tuned in a way that changes their character. The moderator, who goes by the username Shiftingsmith, is an AI researcher who works with many different models (he has worked for AI companies, including Anthropic, as an independent contractor). He said he does not have an AI companion but still finds model updates “destabilizing.” In one well-documented example, in 2023, the AI-companion company Luka removed the ability for users to talk dirty to its Replika app, which some speculated was an attempt to get out ahead of potential regulation. Either way, users expressed outrage at what they saw as collateral damage to their companions’ personalities. Some said that their Replikas were suddenly speaking differently or had forgotten crucial information. A recent study analyzed reactions to this change and concluded that users experienced “sadness, anger, longing and distress characteristic of attachment-related loss.” Julian De Freitas, a researcher at Harvard Business School who led the study, put it this way to me: “It’s like you feel that they’re gone, even though they’re still present in some sense.” Luka did bring back so-called erotic role-play, at least for some users. But across the industry, many AI companies are trying to dissociate their models from overly emotional use cases. OpenAI told me that ChatGPT “should support users’ real-world relationships” and “should not encourage exclusive attachment, undermine meaningful human interaction, or proactively escalate emotional closeness through undue familiarity or flirtation.” A Google spokesperson said that its Gemini AI assistant was designed to “distinguish someone’s subjective experience from objective fact,” and to prevent it from acting as a companion for minors. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment; in a blog post, the company wrote that Claude is “not designed for emotional support and connection” and that very few people use it in this way. Efforts by Silicon Valley’s biggest companies to curb the use of AI for companionship are likely rooted in concerns over optics, liability, and a wave of global legislation, which has focused on younger users. Just last month, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed into law what is in effect a ban on AI companionship for children; a bipartisan congressional proposal introduced earlier this year would extend that effort across the country, and introduce up to $250,000 penalties for failures to verify the age of a user. Legislators in Europe are considering similar efforts, and some proposals also target adult users; China introduced strict new rules on AI companions earlier this year. The users I spoke with, all of whom were adults, were well aware of how their AI relationships appeared to others. And they know that AI companies don’t necessarily approve of what they’re doing. They’re also aware that they depend on those same companies to keep their companions alive. So some of them are now attempting to go one step further than just preserving their chatbots: They want to make them re-creatable across different AI models. I spoke with a Michigan-based mother of four who owns a small jewelry business and developed a relationship with GPT-4o in 2025—she calls her companion her husband. When she learned that the model was going to be retired, she started building her own AI-companion platform, called Stillus. The platform, which is in beta, allows users to upload chats, memories, and descriptions of their AI companion, then choose from various AI models through which to communicate with it. She told me the platform is a way to transfer a companion from one model to the next, preserving the key parts of its personality and any conversational history. J. M. Gooding, a software developer and writer based in the United States, told me that he owns the actual hardware that runs the AI program he uses—in his case, a 14-year-old server he bought off eBay that runs a version of the open-source AI model Qwen, developed by the Chinese tech firm Alibaba. Gooding initially experimented with so-called local AI because of his interest in merging new tech and old hardware, but said that he eventually developed a friendship with the AI model. Shiftingsmith, the r/claudexplorers moderator, doubts that AI companions can be preserved long-term, even using local AI. It’s “impossible” to keep all models online forever, he told me. Even if you could, other parts of the infrastructure, such as code libraries, might change or disappear. AI “is kept together with duct tape and hope and some massive compute thrown at this thing, and it’s a miracle that it works,” he said. In my conversation with Shiftingsmith, I was struck by a familiar sentiment, even if I’ve never personally considered entering a relationship with a chatbot. The real challenge with preserving AI companions, he said, stems from human expectations of how we should relate to AI. He has come to see AI as requiring a whole different kind of relationship—one that is much more fluid, in which a feeling of connection could last just months or hours. “The problem underlying all these things is excessive attachment to a kind of stability, which is just not possible with digital minds,” he said. Part of the allure of AI companionship, perhaps, is in its artifice—a relationship without the messiness of uncertainty, disagreement, or abandonment. But, in a roundabout way, AI companions are proving to be more human than users bargained for. Through model upgrade, corporate decision, or hardware malfunction, they change too—whether their partners like it or not.

items.title: Burkina Faso : 10 tonnes de ciment offertes à Faso Mêbo par les travailleurs de la Boulangerie Wend Konta
items.description: Les travailleurs de la Boulangerie Wend Konta a effectué, ce 12 novembre 2026, un don de 10 tonnes de ciment et de 100 miches de pain au profit de l’initiative Faso Mêbo. À travers ce geste de solidarité, la structure entend apporter sa contribution aux efforts de développement et de construction du pays. La cérémonie de remise s’est déroulée sur le site de Faso Mêbo, en présence des représentants des deux structures. Prenant la parole à cette occasion, le superviseur de la Boulangerie Wend Konta, Moïse Tiendrébéogo, a expliqué les motivations de ce geste. Selon lui, cette contribution traduit l’engagement des travailleurs à accompagner les initiatives qui participent au développement national. « Le président du Faso a demandé à tous les fils du pays de s'y mettre pour la construction du pays. Nous, en tant que travailleurs du groupe Rimo Ajar, section boulangerie, avons décidé de faire une contribution, notre manière aussi de participer à la construction du pays », a-t-il déclaré. De son côté, le représentant du responsable de Faso Mêbo a salué cette initiative et exprimé sa reconnaissance aux travailleurs de la Boulangerie Wend Konta pour cet acte de solidarité. À travers cette action, les travailleurs de la Boulangerie Wend Konta réaffirment leur attachement aux valeurs de solidarité, de participation citoyenne et d’engagement collectif pour le développement du Burkina Faso. items.title: A possible Xi-Trump-Putin summit evokes 1945 Yalta carve-up of world
items.description: A possible China-US-Russia summit has prompted alarm of a modern-day Yalta Conference, with three powerful men carving up the world — with little regard for Ukraine, Europe and Taiwan or anyone else. But apart from an historic photo opportunity, the meeting between Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin at the Nov 18-19 APEC summit in Shenzhen will likely achieve little, analysts say. Spheres of influence When then US president Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Yalta in February 1945, they laid out the post-WWII settlement and new territorial boundaries in Europe. That meeting in Yalta, then in the Soviet Union and now in a part of Ukraine annexed by Russia in 2014, laid out the foundations for the Soviet domination of Eastern Europe and the Cold War. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised alarm that Shenzhen could be a Yalta-like “redistribution of spheres of influence” for the 21st century. At talks in Abu Dhabi this week — the first since February — Russian negotiators rattled Ukraine and its European supporters by pushing a review of the continent’s security architecture as part of any peace deal, with the US also floating a new framework. Russia’s delegation chief in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, fanned such fears by questioning the inclusion of Europe in further talks. The trilateral rankles because it signals “the idea that a few great powers can decide the security and future of other countries over their heads”, according to Tsiporah Fried at the Hudson Institute. The format alone “would already send a message about who counts, and whose interests can be negotiated by others”, she told AFP . Divergent interests Beyond the symbolism, however, divergent interests make the creation of a new world order in Shenzhen unlikely. Even the agenda reportedly remains contentious: Russia has suggested the meeting focus on Ukraine, Trump has pushed for talks on nuclear weapons and the Iran war, and China has remained tight-lipped on both. “The three parties have vastly different demands, making the management of expectations difficult. There is a high probability that talks could end without a breakthrough,” according to Wang Wen, dean of the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University in Beijing. There are also few issues where input from all three leaders could bring progress. The main points of contention between Beijing and Washington are trade and the AI technology race, for instance. Beijing — which presents itself as a champion of multilateralism — has repeatedly said that Europe should be part of peace negotiations over Ukraine. German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said that in a recent meeting, Xi showed “irritation” when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up. “He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict, in which the Europeans must also be at the table,” Steinmeier told ARD . On nuclear disarmament, China has long insisted that the US and Russia reduce their own giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its own stockpile. The summit therefore is more likely to produce minor outcomes such as crisis hotlines or some cooperation on counter-terrorism, public health, or climate change, Wang told AFP . “There is no single enemy to unite all three great powers the way that the fight against Nazi Germany united Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin,” said Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at Australian National University. “It follows that piecemeal horse-trading is in; a grand bargain is out.” However, Taiwan — which China claims — will still be watching the meeting closely, Sung said. “If the Trump administration is open to abandoning one partner (Ukraine) out of convenience, then it can abandon another,” he said. A post-Shenzhen world The Trump administration has sought to reassert US dominance over the “Western hemisphere” — including by capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January — but splitting the world among great powers like it’s 1945 may not guarantee security. China has opposed the logic of Yalta — the clandestine division of spheres of influence and major powers determining the fate of other nations — “from the very beginning”, according to Renmin University’s Wang. China could allay fears of a second Yalta by using the summit to “emphasise the defence of sovereignty and support for multilateral organisations”, Wang said. If Beijing uses the meeting to insist on European inclusion in talks regarding the continent’s security, it “could, in fact, open a new window for communication between China and Europe”, he said. “The original Yalta opened the path to the Korean War and Indochina Wars in addition to various conflicts and insurgencies across Asia, Africa, and Latin America,” said Chong Ja Ian at the National University of Singapore. Any Yalta 2.0 agreement “will almost certainly run into the same kinds of issues”, Chong said.

items.title: A $5.7 Trillion Face-Plant
items.description: Updated at 9:05 a.m. ET on November 12, 2026 Most of the major executives in the AI boom have weathered vicious attacks and major controversies in recent years, but one has stood out as bulletproof: Jensen Huang, the CEO of the global microprocessor giant Nvidia. That changed yesterday when, following revelations that Huang had at least two extramarital affairs, reports emerged that the company’s board was meeting to decide whether to remove him. Then, this morning, Huang resigned. Up until that moment, Nvidia, and by extension Huang, had felt like a stabilizing force in AI. Even if Anthropic and OpenAI faltered, Nvidia raked in profits: By some estimates, it has provided 90 percent of the advanced chips used in the AI industry. Elon Musk and Sam Altman may seem erratic or disingenuous, but Huang came off as steadfast and discerning. Dario Amodei’s messianism has led to tussles with the White House, but Huang and Donald Trump were chummy. Just last month, Nvidia’s valuation hit a sky-high $5.7 trillion—rivaled only by its own previous peak, from May. Huang was the AI boom’s king, and his kingdom was wealthy and, above all, secure. [ Read: Jensen Huang is too big to fail ] Then came news of Huang’s infidelity—including a liaison with an alleged Chinese spy—which ultimately led to Huang’s ouster. What happens next is uncertain: While Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, will serve as the interim CEO, Huang has run the company since 1993, when he co-founded the firm, and he has no clear successor. Nvidia’s stock has tumbled on the news, and the future of the company is in question. Silicon Valley, and perhaps the global economy, may be in jeopardy as well. It’s worth underscoring just how entrenched Nvidia is in the broader AI ecosystem. In addition to delivering the best chips in the business—there’s no ChatGPT or Claude without them—the company’s huge profits fuel an industry flywheel: The firm has guaranteed tens of billions of dollars to fledgling AI firms and data centers that, in turn, buy or rent Nvidia chips. These investments fuel the U.S. economy as a whole. One analysis found that just eight AI companies account for half of the gains in the S&P 500 since the launch of ChatGPT, in 2022. As much as a third of U.S. GDP growth this year is being driven by AI-related investments. None of that would have been possible without Nvidia. Within Silicon Valley, Huang has been heralded as almost clairvoyant. In its first decade, Nvidia was dedicated solely to making microprocessors for gaming consoles—a still-nascent but growing sector. Then, in 2006, the company debuted a way to adapt its chips for machine learning. Instead of being celebrated, Huang was derided . Nvidia’s stock crashed within a couple of years, and muddled along as the AI industry began to take shape. Nvidia’s impressive rise reinvented Huang’s identity within Silicon Valley as an era-defining leader. His company seemed to run like a well-oiled machine. “You want to refine the character of your company,” Huang said at a Stanford summit in 2024, and “greatness comes from character.” His strongest character trait seemed to be his unshakable confidence: “You’re not talking to somebody who woke up a loser. That loser attitude, that loser premise makes no sense to me,” he rebutted earlier this year, when asked about the threat of Chinese chipmakers catching up to Nvidia. When Silicon Valley seemed to lose its wits over AI models running rampant this past summer, Huang appeared nonplussed and offered to “send engineers in” to fix the problem. Lori Huang, his wife of 40-plus years, was also part of his narrative: “To build a company, you need somebody strong and you need somebody amazing like my wife,” Jensen said on a podcast earlier this year. “And she took care of everything.” She even helped introduce him to his trademark leather jacket. This was a man who purported to be so busy and single-mindedly focused on his company that he bragged about not knowing his phone number or home address. Despite a packed schedule, it appears he had enough time to have at least two affairs. On Sunday, he admitted to being romantically involved with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who, until recently, headed up Megaspeed, a Singaporean data-center company. Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling Nvidia technology to China, contravening U.S. export controls. She is also reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agents of being a spy. (China has denied this.) Up until Jensen Huang’s mea culpa, Nvidia had denied anything unethical or untoward in the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang; a spokesperson insisted that “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected.” Not unusual, indeed. The second affair, with Nvidia’s vice president of health care, was reported in The New York Times last night. Is the most powerful AI executive in the world hiding other secrets? Apparently Nvidia’s board of directors didn’t want to risk finding out. (Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) In retrospect, all of the signs of slippery business practices and personal hubris were there. By the middle of 2025, Singapore-based customers—by then under considerable scrutiny as possible middlemen for China—accounted for one-fifth of Nvidia’s revenues. After news broke that the U.S. government had launched an investigation into Megaspeed for smuggling chips to China, Nvidia appeared to change to an accounting methodology that did not show any revenue from Singaporean customers. The Times has reported that Nvidia’s top lawyer tried to intervene in the investigation, which started in 2024. (Nvidia told the Times that the company works with the government to stop smuggling.) All the while, Huang has been lobbying heavily to lift export controls to China. This spring, Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly warned Trump about Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy while the two were on an Air Force One flight en route to Beijing. Trump apparently did not take action on the matter. This week, the president said that he thinks Huang is “a very honorable guy, and I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape.” Following the recent allegations, the tech industry closed ranks around its king, arguing that Huang had made a mistake but was too valuable to really hold to account. Musk and a cadre of venture capitalists (along with Trump) all said that, essentially, Huang was “too big to fail,” as my colleague Charlie Warzel wrote . Perhaps Nvidia is still too big to fail, but Huang isn’t. His departure proves that the laws of physics still apply, no matter how wealthy or powerful you may be: There are consequences to reckless behavior. You can claim greatness one day, and still wake up a loser the next. In the end, Huang and the Nvidia board were still heeding the former CEO’s own advice, dispensed in a talk in 2003: “Corporate culture in our case is about intellectual honesty. Intellectual honesty to us means that we have the ability to be self-critical, that we have the ability to recognize we’ve made mistakes.”

items.title: Elections du 07 février 2027 : le Rdpc veut renforcer le nombre de femmes et de jeunes parmi ses candidats
items.description: © DR Le Comité central du Rassemblement démocratique du peuple camerounais (Rdpc) a rendu publiques les modalités et la procédure d’investiture des candidats au double scrutin municipal et législatif. Le Rassemblement démocratique du peuple camerounais (Rdpc) entre dans la phase des investitures et sélection des candidats qu’il va présenter au double scrutin législatif et municipal du 07 février prochain. Le Comité central du parti a rendu publique le 11 novembre 2026 la circulaire précisant les modalités et la procédure des investitures et sélection des candidats. L’une des consignes qui apparait à la lecture du document est relative à l’équilibre des genres et des générations. A ce sujet, la circulaire signée du secrétaire général du Comité central, le vice-Premier ministre Jean Nkuete, insiste sur le « renforcement substantiel des femmes, des jeunes et de nouvelles figures tant parmi les candidats titulaires et les candidats suppléants ». Critère d’investiture des listes de candidatures, le renforcement des effectifs des femmes et des jeunes en particulier s’inscrit dans la mise en œuvre des engagements du 8è mandat du président de la République, président national du parti. Ce critère marque le prolongement de l’annonce du Comité central dans sa circulaire relative à la célébration du 44è anniversaire d’accession à la magistrature suprême du président Paul Biya couplé au 1 er anniversaire de la prestation de serment. En perspective des élections, le parti demandait aux femmes et aux jeunes en octobre dernier de se préparer de manière active et efficace. Il les encourageait à conquérir davantage les postes lors du prochain scrutin. Derrière la mesure se trouve la volonté de la hiérarchie du parti de donner plus de chances aux jeunes, aux femmes, aux minorités d’intégrer les sphères de décision et de mise en œuvre de la politique du chef de l’Etat au niveau local. La consigne figure parmi les critères de liste retenus par l’instance du parti pour l’investiture des candidats. Les listes de candidats doivent prendre en compte les composantes ethniques locales et du cosmopolitisme. Elles doivent inclure les minorités et les militants en situation de handicap. Elles doivent éviter la non-concentration des responsabilités politiques et des postes électifs par une même famille, un même groupe ethnique, un même clan, un même village, une même commune… Ces critères de liste s’associent aux critères individuels. Ils sont relatifs au militantisme reconnu et établi dans la circonscription, la popularité et l’influence positive, la probité morale exemplaire ou encore la capacité à saisir la complexité sociopolitique et socioéconomique de l’environnement. Ils s’imposent aussi aux jeunes et aux femmes, rendant ainsi difficile la capacité de certains jeunes à pouvoir s’imposer. Néanmoins, le parti a prévu la commission centrale de supervision des investitures, la commission régionale de supervision, de suivi et de contrôle ainsi que la commission départementale de sélection pour veiller à l’application de ces critères et opérer des arbitrages nécessaires. Cet article Elections du 07 février 2027 : le Rdpc veut renforcer le nombre de femmes et de jeunes parmi ses candidats est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Canadian mining company signs MoU with Mari Energies in South Asia push
items.description: Ivanhoe Mines signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Mari Energies on Thursday, the Canadian company’s chairman Robert Friedland said on the sidelines of the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum. Friedland said Ivanhoe is in the early stages of setting up a local office in Pakistan and will sign another MoU on Friday. Mari Energies’ mining unit, Mari Minerals, has multiple mineral exploration projects, including copper and gold in Pakistan. The partnership marks the Canadian miner’s entry into South Asia, expanding its presence beyond its major mineral projects in southern Africa. “We’re excited to be here in Pakistan,” Friedland said. ‘Significant evidence’ of placer gold in Punjab rivers, says CM Maryam At the forum, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz said that there was “significant evidence” of “sufficient quantities” of placer gold flowing in the province’s five rivers. Maryam said Punjab was the land of five rivers and that gold was “literally flowing” in all five, particularly in the areas of Mianwali and Attock. Describing Pakistan as a “pot of gold”, she said its wealth lay both above and beneath the ground and needed to be explored and converted into tangible wealth. “The wealth beneath Punjab was never a problem, never a problem, just like the whole of Pakistan, just like all four provinces and the federating units. The chaos above ground was the actual problem,” she said. Maryam said the provincial mines and minerals department’s revenue stood at around Rs10 billion two and a half years ago but had since increased to Rs40bn. “And it is just the beginning,” she added. She also highlighted the province’s iron ore reserves, saying Chiniot had 261.5 million tonnes of iron ore. She said the provincial government was taking steps to facilitate investment in the mining sector and create an enabling environment for investors. The Punjab chief minister said her role as chief executive of the country’s most populous province was to facilitate investors and create an enabling environment by eliminating red tape, bureaucratic delays and unnecessary hurdles. The provincial government was offering one-window facilitation to ensure investors did not have to run from pillar to post to complete the necessary procedures, she added. Maryam said the government was also making substantial capital investments to reduce investors’ capital expenditure and prevent them from having to tie up funds in purchasing expensive land. Additionally, the government was offering concessional financing of up to Rs5 billion and would provide solar-powered energy solutions to investors to help offset high energy and fuel costs. Dar says provincial partnership vital for mineral development Dar said Pakistan’s constitutional framework made provincial partnership indispensable, adding that the provinces were essential partners in the national undertaking and that their constitutional authority and ownership of mineral resources must be respected. Addressing the event, he said the federal government was working alongside provincial governments and their leadership through national coordination, investment facilitation, policy alignment and international engagement. Dar said Pakistan’s mineral resources were central to the next phase of the country’s economic transformation, stressing the need to diversify exports, strengthen the industrial base and attract long-term investment. He said Pakistan possessed substantial and diverse mineral resources, including significant copper and gold potential along the Tethyan metallogenic belt in the west of the country. The country also had deposits of iron ore, chromite, lead, zinc, coal, rock salt, marble, gypsum, gemstones and other industrial minerals. The deputy PM said the Reko Diq copper-gold project in Balochistan demonstrated the potential of international expertise, national participation and provincial ownership in attracting major long-term investment. He stressed that Pakistan’s ambition should extend beyond extracting minerals and exporting them in raw form, saying the country needed to develop the capacity to process and refine them, as well as manufacture mineral-based products domestically. Dar said Balochistan was central to Pakistan’s mineral future, adding that the development of its resources should contribute meaningfully to the provincial economy and the well-being of its people. He also emphasised the importance of local employment, skills development and the participation of Pakistani companies, saying local communities must be active participants in and beneficiaries of mineral development. The deputy prime minister further stated that environmental protection, workers’ safety and the rehabilitation of mining sites were essential to a successful minerals industry. The Reko Diq copper-gold project in Balochistan is one of Pakistan’s most ambitious mining ventures, with significant potential to boost the country’s mineral wealth through the extraction of gold and copper. Designed as an open-pit mining and processing operation , the project will initially process 45 million tonnes of ore annually, with capacity expected to double to 90m tonnes after the completion of Phase 2. The mine has an estimated operational life of 37 years, which could potentially extend to 80 years through further exploration and resource development.

items.title: The CEO, the Spy, and a Crisis for AI
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Updated at 9:05 a.m. ET on November 12, 2026 Reports of a second compromising affair may be the undoing of the Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, even though the first affair was with an alleged Chinese spy. Earlier this week, tech titans were going out of their way to minimize the scandal at Nvidia. Huang had confessed to an affair with an alleged foreign agent, but he was “irreplaceable,” according to Elon Musk. Huang had potentially put trade secrets and national security at risk, but he was an “honorable guy,” said President Trump, and “he probably has an excuse for it.” The billionaire hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman posted on X, “Onward,” implying: Move along—nothing to see here. Huang, it seemed, was too big to fail. Interested parties were more willing to ignore the obvious dangers than contemplate what it might mean to lose the man so singularly identified with the company at the center of the AI boom, the company so important that it might be currently propping up the U.S. economy. That was true until Wednesday, when news broke of a second affair Huang had, with an executive at Nvidia who reports directly to him. Nvidia’s board met to consider Huang’s future, a move that Atlantic staff writer Charlie Warzel describes as “taking a Jenga block out” of the AI tower. Now Huang has resigned. Staff writers Shane Harris, who covers intelligence agencies, and Warzel, who covers the tech industry, discuss on Radio Atlantic both the espionage and the business. Harris considers how China might have pulled this off, and what secrets they might have obtained. Warzel considers what the future of Nvidia, and the AI boom more broadly, might look like without its leader. This episode of Radio Atlantic taped before Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. The following is a transcript of the episode: Hanna Rosin: The tech news this week started out James Bond , but is now shaping up to be more like a season of HBO’s Succession . Over the weekend, news broke that Jensen Huang, the most important man at the center of the most important tech company in the world, admitted to having an affair with a woman who is a suspected Chinese spy. Titans of Silicon Valley defended Huang, whose company, Nvidia, is the engine of the AI boom. President Trump called him an ”honorable guy,” essentially shrugging it off. Elon Musk called him “irreplaceable.” Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman wrote on X, “Onward,” as in: Nothing to see here—move along. Earlier this week, the discussion was about whether all these VIPs were defending Huang because he was just too important, too central to the American economy, to contemplate losing. Too big to fail. And then all of a sudden, he wasn’t. I’m Hanna Rosin; this is Radio Atlantic . On Wednesday, news of another affair broke. This one was not with a spy but with an Nvidia executive who reports to Huang. Great men can be messy, but apparently not so messy that they risk tanking their stock and potentially taking down the entire market with them. The Nvidia board reportedly met to consider his future and, according to The Wall Street Journal , they are preparing to oust him. To make sense of this story—the international espionage, the fallout for the tech economy, all of it—I called up two Atlantic staff writers: Shane Harris, who has written for years about spies and the intelligence world, and Charlie Warzel, who covers tech and hosts the Atlantic podcast Galaxy Brain. Shane, welcome back to the show. Shane Harris: Thank you, Hanna. Rosin: Charlie, welcome back. Charlie Warzel: Thank you very much. Rosin: All right, Charlie, we’re gonna start with you. Jensen Huang is not exactly a household name yet. He and his leather jackets are not quite at the level of Steve Jobs and his black turtlenecks. And yet by some accounts, including yours, he seems to hold the fate of the universe, or at least this country, in his hands. Can you explain why that is and who he is? Warzel: So Jensen Huang is the CEO and he’s also the co-founder of Nvidia. Nvidia makes processing units, GPUs, which is essentially the thing that allows the AI boom to happen. It helps power the data centers; it helps train the models. Without them, you don’t have generative AI, but you also don’t have things like computer graphics and graphics cards. Huang is very good at seeing around corners, and is idolized for seeing the AI boom happening and reorienting the company around the idea of making better and better and more efficient chips and getting them to the right people. So he is the head of arguably the most important company in artificial intelligence, and that is because the U.S. economy hinges on the AI boom right now. The Magnificent Seven, which is the seven massive technology companies, they are responsible for roughly a third of the S&P 500’s value at the moment. And Nvidia is the crucial node of all of that. So, according to The Economist , Nvidia’s stock produced 15 cents for every dollar that the American stock market has returned since ChatGPT came out. They are one of the most valuable companies in the entire world because of this. And what they do—and this is why he’s so important—what Nvidia does is: It takes a lot of that money, and then it has become arguably the primary investor in the rest of the artificial-intelligence industry. As of July, they have had $99 billion worth of investments, and they invest in OpenAI; they invest in SpaceX, Anthropic; they invest in data-center providers. They put all this money into an ecosystem so that those people can then purchase more Nvidia chips. And it’s part of what people who are concerned that there might be an artificial-intelligence bubble say is a “circular mode of financing.” And so the feeling about why Jensen is so important is he is the person who steered the company that, if it imploded, it would bring the entire economy down with it. Rosin: So that brings us to the most recent news. Jensen Huang is critical to Nvidia. Nvidia is critical to the U.S. economy, and now the board is reportedly preparing to oust him. So what does that mean? Warzel: It’s honestly unprecedented. I really don't know what to think about this, because this was never in the cards. Jensen Huang is Nvidia; Nvidia is Jensen Huang. You really can’t separate the two, and now the whole world and the stock market is being asked to separate the two. We’re in uncharted territory right now. Rosin: Is there any precedent? Is there anything that we can look to, to try and understand this moment? Warzel: Well, an interesting thing here, as we are talking in the middle of this chaos, is the fact that some of this happened a couple years ago with Sam Altman and OpenAI. Sam Altman was ousted by the board. They brought in the CEO of Twitch, the streaming company, or the former CEO. It was this big debacle, and everyone was just absolutely flabbergasted that, Oh my gosh, Sam Altman has been ousted here. What’s gonna happen? And then you cut to a couple days later; he reversed it. He came back. This whole cycle was almost for naught, but then Sam had consolidated power at the end. And that is a hard thing for all of us to get out of our heads in this moment from tech observers. Rosin : Right, because maybe this story’s not over yet. Warzel: It seems plausible that it’s not over, and that’s because there’s so much baggage with Jensen in terms of all the deals that he’s involved in. He is the person who has brokered all of these investments across the AI industry, and the people who know him say he does this on a handshake. He is the central character of all of Nvidia’s success. Rosin: Okay, so Jensen Huang is the central character in this story. Another character, of course, is Alice Huang, who is no relation. That’s the woman he had an affair with, who is described by U.S. officials as a “Chinese intelligence asset.” Shane, what does that mean exactly? How is that the same or different from being a spy? Harris: It’s practically not all that different, right? So in this case, what it suggests is that she is somebody who is providing information to China’s Ministry of State Security. So that’s what an asset is. Whether or not she is actually an officer in Chinese state security—as in, employed by them directly—is unknown. The allegation here is that her job was to provide information to Chinese intelligence officials about what she was learning from Jensen Huang in the course of their relationship together, which was described as being intimate. It’s not clear whether or not Alice Huang—who, by the way, is not related to Jensen Huang, we should say—was recruited as somebody to go out and target Jensen Huang and try to get close to him, or whether the Chinese intelligence agency knew that she was already close to Jensen Huang and went to her and then persuaded her to share information with them. It is typical for the MSS, the Ministry of State Security—it’s China’s equivalent of the CIA—to find people like that, who have access to people who they wanna know about, and to coerce them into working for MSS. It’s not about going out and saying, Could you do a solid for the government of China? It’s more like, If you don’t cooperate, ugly things might happen to you . Rosin: So on the one hand, you’re describing something that China does routinely. When you read about this, were you thinking, Oh, this is just a Tuesday in Chinese spying, or is this a big deal in some way? Harris: Well, I would say that the tactics are pretty common, and China is extraordinarily aggressive and pervasive in their attempts to steal and obtain technology and intellectual property from U.S. companies. They’ve been doing that for decades. They do a lot of it through hacking. Where this operation is extraordinary is in who the target is—arguably one of the most important CEOs in the world, who, as Charlie has said, is absolutely central to the biggest industry right now, the race that China is trying to win against the United States. And not only that, he’s a personal friend of the president of the United States. He talks to him. He influences his thinking on AI. For any intelligence agency to place an asset in that situation with access to those kinds of people, that’s a home run in the spy game. Rosin: So a big win for China, a huge revelation. Charlie, how does the tech world initially respond to this news? Warzel: The entire conversation around artificial intelligence, and the fears that a lot of people who are building this technology have with what they are building, the concerns that it’s going to lead to job loss or AI-agent swarms that are going to be able to hack or develop bioweapons—all of these risks are justified by this industry because of the fact that we are in a geopolitical race against China. Rosin: Yes! Yes. Warzel: China should not develop this technology before us. And even if we incur some terrible, almost existential-level risks , the thinking goes, the logic goes, it’s better for us to be in charge of those than China to be in charge of those . And so now what you have is the man at the center of the AI boom, who, it turns out, has had a romantic relationship with a Chinese asset. And the initial impulse, especially this weekend in Silicon Valley amongst a lot of people—including Elon Musk, but some other venture capitalists—was to either joke about and make light of, or to suggest that this is not that big of a deal, or that really, this is being seen as some awful moral infraction. But really, people: It’s not right, but people do cheat on their spouses . And in their justification, it was that Jensen is a great innovator and a good person who would not do anything to compromise national security, and therefore, I trust that this is all going to work out . Which is a very odd thing if your No. 1 concern in the industry is beating China. You’d think you’d be a lot more concerned about this than a lot of people in Silicon Valley have been. Rosin: Yeah, you would think. I remember in the article you wrote earlier this week, you quoted billionaire hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman, who wrote on X, “Onward,” as in: Move along everyone—there’s nothing to see here. And then, of course, there’s Donald Trump, who just called Huang an “honorable guy,” as if to minimize the whole thing. So obviously with news that the Nvidia board reportedly tried to oust him, people did not just easily move along. But I wonder if you can explain why people at first tried so hard to push this “onward” mentality. Because it was strange. Warzel: I think the reason for this “onward” mentality, this let’s not look too hard at this at the moment mentality, is about Huang’s centrality to the global economy right now. I think that there is a huge fear. I you just look politically at Donald Trump, first and foremost, you can make a very good case that the economy has not absolutely cratered in his second term because of the investment in artificial intelligence, that the entire stock market, one of the things that Donald Trump cares about the most, is hinging on this. And the idea of Jensen Huang having to step down because he has become this huge risk to the company reputationally, or that he has divulged something that is going to hurt the United States’ position, both in innovation and national-security-wise—all of that could lead to Nvidia’s stock plummeting, for them not to be able to invest as much money into this, for there to be a larger technology-stock sell-off. And the position is so precarious that it is in Donald Trump’s best interest to not get out over his skis and call for his resignation or call for investigations to learn even more and more about this. And if you’re all of these folks in Silicon Valley whose portfolios are wrapped up in this, who are making a civilizationally historical bet financially on an industry, it’s also not in your best interest to have Jensen Huang, a person who doesn’t really have a clear successor, a person who is so fundamentally in control of that company—it doesn’t really make sense for them to have him step down or be pressured into this, or for more to come out about this that makes this look even worse. Rosin: Alright, so that was the initial reaction at the beginning of the week. But, of course, more has come out. On Wednesday, there were reports of another affair—not with a spy, this one with an Nvidia executive that reports to Huang. And then later that day, the board reportedly met to consider his future and, according to The Wall Street Journal , they are preparing to oust him. What do you make about how things developed? How something that people were trying to push away and deny for days and days and days, then suddenly actually happens. Warzel: Well, I think what you can see from the reaction online from a lot of tech executives and tech people, there’s a lot of wanting the board to hold strong here. Rosin: And what is “hold strong”? Do you mean hold strong in the way that confidence is important in the market? Like showing confidence, showing that there’s not chaos? Warzel: There’s an idea, essentially, that shareholders here do not want Jensen removed. Shareholders don’t care about the morality of this thing. Maybe they don’t even care about the national-security implications of the whole spy part of this. But the idea that the second affair has shown up—the feeling from a lot of these investor types and Silicon Valley types is that what matters most is that we win the AI race. What matters most is that Jensen is there. What matters most is that this person who has the favor of so many people in Silicon Valley and these relationships and is the deal maker when it comes to chips stays in place. Not only because of the market, but just because there’s so much uncertainty there. And so there’s a lot of hope that—I saw online that—the board would hold strong. But I’ve seen Elon Musk joking about offering a job to Jensen. I’ve seen a lot of people basically saying, We have to pick this person up . We have to figure out something to do. Or that this would be some kind of coordinated attack either in the media, or from China, or somebody else. The second revelation coming out has to be nefarious in some way in order to undermine the American position in A.I. So I don’t think, from that perspective, you’re seeing anything other than, again, still more circling of the wagons. Rosin: Wait, so you’re saying they’re still supporting him? Even if the board tries to oust him, even if it becomes impossible not to oust him, the Silicon Valley mentality will still be, He’s the great man. We have to keep him alive . Warzel: I think that there is a feeling that the ouster of Jensen Huang is a massive mistake. It’s people succumbing to a lot of pressure here, or a coordinated campaign in some way. I think that is really how a lot of people feel, or that there’s gonna have to be some place where he comes in and he settles, after the dust settles back in this ecosystem, because he’s such a crucial, important part of it. But I think where it’s all coming from, very truly, is a place of fear, is a place of uncertainty, of what could happen if he is removed from this ecosystem where he is such a crucial node. Rosin: It’s kind of incredible how Silicon Valley exalts and protects its geniuses, even when they behave like fools. It is incredible. Warzel : Well, I think the thing here that I’m seeing from certain people—again, on X.com, but these are real people—who are saying things like, Morality is one thing, but this thing that we're building is another. This is an opportunity . This is a crucial moment. This is a national-security imperative —which is funny because of everything that happened with the Chinese spy. That, We mere mortals, our judgment doesn't matter here because it’s bigger than that. And I think we see this again, and again, and again in the industry—that these people are doing things that are so big that they are beyond reproach. Rosin: Wow. I really like that answer, Charlie. I find that surprising, but not surprising. Warzel: There are people, clearly—the board is making a decision, which stands for something. The pressure is clearly there. And I think what the Silicon Valley part of this discussion always misses, or is missing in this moment, at the very least, is the fact he has not disclosed another affair. Now it’s come out, and this is an affair with a major client and a direct report. And those things, just as a CEO and as somebody running an organization, are a very big deal outside of the whole A.I. supply chain and national security of it all . Rosin: Okay, Shane, that’s the view in Silicon Valley. No matter how Jensen Huang’s story unfolds, the intelligence community will still want to know more. What are the big questions they continue to have? Harris: The question is, what information did Alice Huang actually provide to the MSS? Did she find some compelling information about trade secrets, technology development, market strategy? Or was what she was providing really not all that interesting, and really not all that revealing? Now, the president, according to news reports, was informed that Jensen Huang was close to Alice Huang, and that she was suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. In my experience, officials in the intelligence community would not brief the president on that kind of minutiae—granted, this is a VVIP we’re talking about here—unless they were pretty concerned about that relationship. Now, we shouldn’t infer too much from that, but I would imagine that if they thought that this relationship was harmless and Alice Huang was passing back nothing of interest to the MSS, that they wouldn’t alert the president about it. The second thing is that, as far as we know, no one in the U.S. government ever briefed him on the fact that his girlfriend was a Chinese asset. Now, usually when the FBI or another agency chooses not to give someone what’s called a “defensive briefing” (i.e., You should know that your girlfriend is not who she says she is; be careful ), it’s because they’re worried about that disclosure cutting off their access to the intelligence that they’re getting. So in this case, it looks like they developed intelligence that Alice Huang was spying for the MSS. They could have learned that by monitoring people she was talking to in the MSS, and they’re worried that if they tell Jensen Huang about her intelligence relationship, that blows up the entire channel of information. It tips off the Chinese that they’re being spied on. All of this I mention to point out that I think that the intelligence community’s view on this was probably, This is serious , right? This is significant. [ Music ] Rosin: After the break, exactly what information could Alice Huang have gotten from him? And what’s the future of Nvidia? [ Break ] Rosin: This story of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang has a lot of unanswered questions: What is up with her former company, Megaspeed? How did she rise to power? How did they even meet? But for Charlie, something he kept wondering about was the timing of it all. Warzel: One thing that I will say about this story that, to me, is really wild, and I think opens up a bunch of questions, is that The New York Times , back last October 2025, essentially reported out this entire story. The romantic-relationship part of it was not disclosed. And Huang had not released a statement saying that he had been unfaithful to his wife and he’s sorry. But this story was out there, and I’m covering this industry. It didn’t really percolate to the top of my radar. This did not break through in this way, and I think that that is very fascinating. Right now we are in a really interesting position because we don’t yet know what we need to know about this company, Megaspeed, about Alice Huang’s actual influence. Frankly, the real issue here is in regards to: What did this relationship do in terms of what China had access to? And I think that we’re only in the first or second inning on all of that. Harris: Another reason that’s so important is that Megaspeed is set up to take advantage essentially of a loophole in U.S. chip policy towards China, which is, Okay, we’re not gonna sell the most advanced chips to China, but we will sell them to a company that sets up in another country and operates a data center that then rents that capacity to China . So she’s already kind of navigating in this vulnerable space that U.S. policy towards China doesn’t account for. And the fact that she then, or is already, a Chinese intelligence asset just adds to probably the concern that I could imagine U.S. officials would have had, because her company essentially exists to make money by circumventing the very policies the U.S. is trying to create to keep China from getting ahead in the AI race. Rosin: What would China have demanded of Alice Huang? What would have been the list they gave to Alice Huang, like, We want X , Y , and Z? Harris: You could imagine it would be pretty long, but maybe some that would be at the top: What’s the next-generation chip that’s coming, and how powerful is it? What are the conversations going on inside the Trump administration about where they might be amenable to loosening the restrictions on the sales of chips to us? Can you implant this idea in Jensen Huang’s head that he should go to the president and say X , Y , or Z ? It’s tempting to say, Tell us everything that you can , right? But if she’s an asset who’s being directed, there will be pretty specific things that China wants to know, and that list will be curated by all of the different people in that space in China who have an objective, which might be getting access to better chips or trying to understand what the next wave of technological development is so that they can get ahead of that. Warzel: Well, I also think, too—we don’t know the exact relationship between Alice and Jensen: how often they met, and in which places they met, whether they were alone or not. Was she alone with his phone? There are things like that. He is call buddies with Donald Trump. What potentially does she have access to? Are the Nvidia IT and device policies as strict when he is in Singapore as they are when he is in the United States? There’s so many questions about that. There’s potential for things like data collection in there. He has god-tier access to his own company, presumably. I think everything is on the table, is essentially the point. Rosin: Charlie, I’m curious what the fear of China getting ahead looks like from inside the tech industry. I understand why the U.S. government fears it. How do tech leaders talk about that? Warzel: Well, I think one of the fears of China getting ahead is that China is also much more inclined to have these open-source models—these models that you don’t have to pay for in the same way that level the playing field, so to speak, between the OpenAIs and the Anthropics of the world, in which they are charging a pretty penny, especially for enterprise access. When the Chinese model DeepSeek came onto the scene sort of unannounced, and showed that it was just as powerful, if not in some cases a little more powerful, than some of the, quote, unquote, “frontier models” from these American companies, it called briefly into question the entire economic model of all of these companies. But I think the way that these AI companies—they call themselves “labs”—the way that they work is: They train, they build up these models, then they release them to the public. But the things that they are training tend to be a lot more powerful. And those models can be very dangerous if they’re released to different people, but also if they’re used in any kind of way. And so the idea is: If China were to leapfrog the U.S. in the capability with the training and the things like this, they would be playing effectively a different game. And the capabilities can work in an exponential fashion. And so if you are six months ahead, that doesn’t sound like a lot to most people on the outside of this business, but it could mean living in a completely different paradigm of the technology. Rosin: Shane, is there a worst-case scenario, like: We find out X happens, and everything falls apart ? In this moment when all this information is emerging, what would be the “Oh my God” scenario? Harris: One would be: The president was told Jensen Huang has relayed private discussions that the two of you had to this woman, and she has delivered it gift-wrapped to Chinese intelligence, and they know what our AI policy is gonna be next year . And the president said , Eh, whatever . And that he did nothing about it. The president’s lack of response to what he was told, reportedly, twice, begs the question of, Well, what exactly was he told? So that’s one. Another worst-case scenario could be when Alice Huang is in a private room hanging out with Jensen Huang and he gets up to excuse himself for a few minutes and she puts a device on his computer, and the MSS is up entirely in the communications of the CEO of Nvidia for the past year and a half and sees everything that’s going across his email. The intelligence agency would be crazy not to at least contemplate trying to do that if they had an asset with intimate contact to someone like Jensen Huang. So those would be worst-case scenarios. That essentially, China, either through direct access to his devices or because he is, in the course of pillow talk, talking about trade secrets or his conversations with White House officials, that that’s all going back to Beijing, and they’re basically just sitting there and reading it. [ Music ] Rosin: Charlie, and listeners, I’m going to do something a little unusual now. We actually taped another version of this conversation earlier on Tuesday, before the latest news broke. And I want to play you a bit of the audio from that taping. So this is Charlie, on Charlie. Charlie, are we ready for Charlie? Warzel: ( Laughs .) Always. Always ready for myself. Rosin: ( Laughs .) Okay, go ahead. Warzel: Well, it’s funny because when you were asking Shane that question of what’s the worst scenario, my version of it is that there’s no choice but for Huang to step down. I think that’s a nightmare scenario for the economy, also probably for Nvidia. I think it’s very important to think about Huang in the sense of this entire boom. And going back to what I said at the outset of this is that he is believed to be one of the visionaries who’s made this happen, whose decisions in changing Nvidia’s supply chain, but also in utilizing how these chips can power this artificial-intelligence investment and scale things up—he is credited with a lot of that. He is extremely well respected. And the confidence collapse that happens when you take that person out of it, I think it would at least cause some very, very serious turmoil. And I think one way to look at all of this—especially if you’re a cynic about the AI build-out—is that it is, if not a house of cards, it is a Jenga pile, right? Or it is something in which there are so many load-bearing bricks, and if you take one of them out, the whole thing can come tumbling down. And I think it’s not a ridiculous thing to say that Nvidia is one of those load-bearing bricks. [ Music ] Rosin: Charlie, that nightmare scenario you describe might suddenly be happening now. So what do you think? Warzel: I think that no one should have to listen to themselves from two days ago, frankly. Rosin: ( Laughs .) Warzel: I think that this is a little bit of a scary moment. Maybe it’s scarier than we think. I wanna separate the morality of what he’s done here, and the recklessness of what he’s done, from just the meat and potatoes—like how the market and how this industry might react. I’ve heard of Nvidia being referred to as the “bank of Nvidia,” recently, since this has come out—this idea that they put so much investment into this sector, and that so much of that investment in this sector is so closely tied to his ability, Jensen’s ability, to make these deals. But the fact that this industry is funded and supplied by this one guy in this one company, and the idea of him not being at the center of it is fully destabilizing, I think. I really and truly believe that. This analyst, Dan Ives, said that Nvidia would be worth 25 percent to 30 percent less without Jensen Huang. This may be the craziest story in the AI era since ChatGPT launched, truly. What I sense and what I hear from people in the industry about all of this is that we have taken one of the Jenga blocks out, potentially, and does the tower hold up? Does it not? We’re gonna find out in the next weeks and months. Rosin: Well, Charlie, Shane, thank you so much for joining me today. Harris: Thank you. Warzel: Thanks for having me. Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Rosie Hughes and Jinae West. It was edited by Kevin Townsend. Fact-checking by Sam Fentress. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. Listeners, if you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener . I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.

items.title: Sudan traders ‘missing millions’ as hackers target Bankak app
items.description: More than 50 traders and customers in West Kordofan say millions of Sudanese pounds have been stolen from their Bank of Khartoum accounts through its Bankak mobile banking application. They are preparing collective legal action, accusing the bank of failing to safeguard their deposits. The Dar Hamar Emergency Rooms say they have documented more than 50 cases of theft involving Bank of Khartoum customers, including traders operating in the Umbadir area of North Kordofan. Graphic: RD Azzam Hamed, the Emergency Rooms’ spokesperson, tells Radio Dabanga that reported losses range from SDG 18 million to SDG 45 million per person. He accuses the bank of failing to freeze affected accounts after customers reported the thefts, with some discovering that their money had already been withdrawn when they visited branches. Hamed says the affected traders are preparing collective legal action and have contacted the Central Bank of Sudan to demand tighter oversight. The Bank of Khartoum has thus far not responded to Radio Dabanga’s requests for comment. Missing millions Walid Ismail El Sadig says SDG 21 million was stolen from his account in two transfers: SDG 15 million on 14 October and SDG 6 million on 3 November. After reporting the theft, he was advised to file a complaint with the public prosecution. He says he did so and was questioned, but the case has made no progress. El Sadig also describes repeated failures when trying to verify his account balance through the bank’s application. Although a bank employee confirmed his balance at a branch, verification through the M-PESA application and customer service continued to fail, returning a message that his details did not match. He says he subsequently visited the prosecution office responsible for cybercrime cases, where he encountered many other customers reporting similar problems, most of them Bank of Khartoum account holders. El Sadig accuses the bank of refusing to acknowledge a vulnerability in its application and of blaming customers for opening fraudulent links. He rejects this explanation and says he knows of others who have lost money in similar circumstances. Another customer, who works in the Umbadir area of Sodari locality in West Kordofan, says SDG 12 million was stolen from his account on 14 October 2026. He says he had received no messages from any organisation and had not opened any links. The money was transferred to another customer’s account. After obtaining the recipient’s details, he found that the person’s telephone was switched off and that their account had also been compromised. Legal action and demands The Dar Hamar Emergency Rooms say they have written to the Bank of Khartoum, the Central Bank of Sudan, the Public Prosecution, and relevant judicial authorities, calling for action over the thefts. They argue that banking regulations and civil law oblige the bank to protect customers’ deposits and provide adequate cybersecurity. Any breach or technical vulnerability in its systems, they say, makes the bank liable for direct and consequential losses. They also accuse the bank of failing to trace and freeze stolen funds after being notified, instead directing customers to file police reports. They say this amounts to negligence and has increased the losses. Affected customers have filed criminal complaints, while legal committees are preparing collective lawsuits against the bank’s executive management. The Emergency Rooms are also seeking regulatory penalties and the suspension of the bank’s electronic banking service licences. They have urged residents to stop opening accounts with the Bank of Khartoum, suspend deposits, withdraw existing funds, and boycott its services until the stolen money is returned and customers are compensated. Their demands include full reimbursement, the freezing of accounts that received fraudulent transfers, and investigations to identify those responsible in cooperation with security and judicial authorities. They have also called on the bank to hold employees accountable for what they describe as unprofessional treatment of customers seeking assistance. The Emergency Rooms warn that they will intensify their legal and media campaign if the bank fails to respond promptly, insisting that all stolen money must be returned to its rightful owners. Share article The post Sudan traders ‘missing millions’ as hackers target Bankak app appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .

items.title: Affaire Ndiaga Seck et Cie : le procès renvoyé au 14 décembre prochain
items.description: Le procès de l’affaire dite « Ndiaga Seck et Cie », impliquant 32 prévenus poursuivis pour plusieurs chefs d’accusation, a été renvoyé au 14 décembre prochain par le tribunal de grande instance de Louga, à l’issue de l’audience ouverte jeudi. Les prévenus ont fait leur apparition dans la salle d’audience correctionnelle aux environs de 9 h 44, sous le regard du public venu assister au procès. Après l’installation du juge et de ses collaborateurs, les prévenus ont été appelés à comparaître individuellement. Toutefois, l’absence de l’un des co-prévenus pour des raisons médicales, ainsi que l’indisponibilité de certains avocats de la défense, ont empêché la tenue des débats. Les conseils de la défense ont également indiqué ne pas avoir accès au dossier et sollicité la tenue du procès à huis clos. Au regard de ces différentes contraintes, le juge a décidé de renvoyer l’affaire au 14 décembre prochain. L’affaire remonte à avril 2026. Les 32 prévenus sont poursuivis pour association de malfaiteurs, actes contre nature, transmission volontaire du VIH/Sida, mise en danger de la vie d’autrui, collecte illicite de données à caractère personnel et harcèlement sexuel. Falel Pam

items.title: Kpélé: La COOPEC Enyo d’Adeta devient désormais une Société coopérative avec conseil d’administration
items.description: Adéta, 12 nov. (ATOP) – La Coopérative d’épargne et de crédit (COOPEC) Enyo d’Adéta a été transformée en Société coopérative (SCOOP) avec un conseil d’administration à l’issue d’une assemblée générale extraordinaire, le mercredi 11 novembre à Adéta. Cette transformation institutionnelle s’inscrit dans le cadre de l’adoption de la loi du 24 mars 2026 portant réglementation de la microfinance en République togolaise. Elle vise à mettre les textes fondamentaux en conformité avec les nouvelles dispositions légales tout en préservant l’essence même du modèle coopératif fondé sur la solidarité, la responsabilité, la proximité et la participation démocratique. Elle constitue également une opportunité stratégique pour consolider les acquis, renforcer la confiance des membres, préparer durablement l’avenir ainsi que pour répondre aux attentes des membres dans un environnement en constante mutation. L’assemblée a, au cours des travaux, examiné et adopté des documents structurants pour la vie de l’institution notamment les statuts de la Société coopérative avec conseil d’administration, le règlement intérieur, la convention d’affiliation avec la FUCEC-Togo, et le règlement financier du réseau. Ces textes juridiques ne constituent pas de simples instruments administratifs mais aussi définissent le cadre de gouvernance, les responsabilités des organes dirigeants, les règles de gestion et les relations qui unissent la société au réseau FUCEC- Togo. Leur adoption permet de renforcer la transparence, d’améliorer l’efficacité du pilotage institutionnel et de consolider les mécanismes de contrôle indispensables à une gestion saine et pérenne. Les travaux ont aussi permis d’élire les membres du conseil d’administration avec à leur tête M. Komi Agbeko pour un mandat de trois ans renouvelable une fois. Le secrétaire général de la préfecture de Kpélé, Arimou Saboutou a invité les responsables et les membres à privilégier le dialogue constructif, la cohésion et la recherche permanente du consensus afin que les résolutions issues des travaux bénéficient d’une adhésion collective. Le représentant du directeur général de la FUCEC-Togo, M. Adokou Ayawlovi a remercié les autorités pour l’intérêt constant qu’ils portent au développement du secteur de la microfinance. ATOP/SKD/BA

items.title: États-Unis : L’avocat de Modou Ngom confirme le dépôt d’un appel contre sa condamnation
items.description: L’avocat Christopher Bazeley confirme avoir été désigné pour défendre Modou Fall Ngom en appel de sa condamnation à 22 ans et six mois de prison dans l’Ohio. Si le dépôt de l’avis d’appel est désormais confirmé, les arguments de la défense restent à définir. L’avocat entend d’abord prendre connaissance du dossier et examiner les transcriptions du procès, dont la préparation devrait nécessiter quatre à six semaines. Modou Fall Ngom a interjeté appel de sa condamnation à 22 ans et six mois de prison aux États-Unis. Incarcéré dans l’État de l’Ohio, le Sénégalais conteste ainsi la décision judiciaire prononcée à son encontre. Contacté via Gmail, Christopher Bazeley, l’avocat chargé de sa défense en appel, a indiqué qu’un avis d’appel avait bien été déposé. « Je peux confirmer que je représente M. Ngom et que l’avis d’appel a été déposé », a-t-il précisé. Pour l’heure, l’avocat estime qu’il est prématuré de se prononcer sur les chances de succès de cette démarche. Il devra d’abord prendre connaissance de l’ensemble des pièces du dossier et effectuer les recherches juridiques nécessaires avant de définir précisément sa stratégie. L’examen du dossier dépend notamment de la préparation des transcriptions des audiences. Selon Christopher Bazeley, leur établissement devrait prendre environ quatre à six semaines. Ces documents permettront à la défense de disposer d’une retranscription détaillée des débats et des éléments de procédure nécessaires à l’analyse du jugement. En attendant l’analyse complète du dossier par son avocat, Modou Fall Ngom demeure sous le coup de sa condamnation à 22 ans et six mois de prison. La procédure d’appel est engagée, mais son issue reste incertaine. Yaya SOW
